Surah Maryam (peace be upon her) is Meccan, except for verses fifty-eight and seventy-one, which are Medinan, and its verses number ninety-eight.

﴿Kaf, Ha, Ya, 'Ayn, Sad.﴾ It is recited with imalah (vowel inclination) of the ha and the ya, with the dal of the sound being made clear. It has also been read with a fatha on the ha, imalah on the ya, and with both emphasized (tafkhim). And with ikhfa' (partial concealment) of the nun before the sad, because the two are close in articulation. It has already been established that these opening letters, which cannot be single letters and have no counterpart to be weighed against, are pronounced only by way of citation (hikayah), with their final letters left quiescent in pause (waqf), whether they are taken as names of the surahs or recited in a sequence of enumeration. Even though this entails the meeting of two quiescent letters, which is excused in the context of pause with certainty, the proper way to pause on this noble opening is to stop on it, following the original form. It has also been read with idgham (assimilation) of the dal into what follows, because the two are close in point of articulation. If it is taken as the name of the surah, as most scholars hold, then its position is nominative (raf'), either as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject, the estimated sense being: "This is Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad," i.e., named by it. The pointing to it was valid even though its mention has not preceded, because by virtue of its being upon the wing of remembrance it has taken the ruling of what is present and witnessed, as one says: "This is what so-and-so bought." Or it is taken as a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is...

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 2:**

﴿The mention of your Lord's mercy﴾. That is, the one named by it is "the mention of the mercy of..." etc. Since the mention of it (the mercy) is the opening of the noble surah, and the main content it contains, it is treated as if it were the mention of itself. The first option is the better one, because what is made the title of a subject should be something whose attribution to it is already known to the addressee, and since there was no prior knowledge of the name, its proper role is to inform about it, as in the first option. If the surah is taken as a sequence of enumerated items, in the manner favored by the scholars of rigorous verification (ahl al-tahqiq), then "ذِكْرُ" (dhikr, "the mention of") is the predicate of an omitted subject, which is what the enumeration of the letters points to, as if it were said: "The composition made of this kind of letters, expanded, intended by it is the surah, the mention of the mercy..." etc. Or it is a demonstrative, indicated by which the subject is pointed to, treating the presence of the material as the presence of the composition made from it, i.e., "This is the mention of the mercy of..." etc. It has been said: it is a subject whose predicate is omitted, i.e., "in what is recited to you is its mention." And it is read "ذَكَرَ رَحْمَةَ رَبِّكَ" (dhakara rahmata rabbika) in the past tense of the causative, i.e., "this recited text mentioned it." And it is read "ذَكِّرْ" (dhakkir) in the imperative. The specification of the attribute of lordship (rububiyya), which indicates the conveyance to perfection, together with its attribution to his pronoun (ﷺ), is to signal that the sending down of the surah upon him (ﷺ) is a completion of him (ﷺ). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿His servant﴾ is an object of "rahmati rabbika" (mercy of your Lord), on the basis that the mercy is an object of what is attributed to it. It has been said: it is an object of "al-dhikr" (the mention), on the basis that it is a verbal noun attributed to its agent in a broadened sense. The meaning of "the mention of the mercy" is its reaching and befalling, as one says: "The kindness of so-and-so mentioned me," i.e., reached me. His saying, mighty and exalted is He: ﴿Zakariyya﴾ is a "badal" (substitute apposition) of it, or an "atf bayan" (explicative apposition) to it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 3:

﴿When he called to his Lord with a secret call.﴾ It is a temporal clause (zarf) governed by "raḥmat rabbika" (the mercy of your Lord). It has also been said that it is governed by "dhikr" (the mention), with the latter taken as a noun annexed to its agent by way of broad usage (ittisā'an), not in the first manner, because of the corruption of the meaning. It has also been said that it is a badal al-ishtimal (substitution of inclusion) from Zakariyya, as in His saying: ﴿And mention in the Book Mary, when she withdrew﴾. Upon him be prayer and peace, he observed the excellence of conduct (husn al-adab) in concealing his supplication. For although, relative to Him, Mighty and Majestic is He, a loud call is like a secret one, the secret call is more inclined to sincerity (ikhlas), further from ostentation (riya'), and closer to safety from the blame of people for seeking a child, since that depends on preliminaries that are not fitting for him to undertake in the time of old age and senility, and from the harm of his clients (mawali) whom he feared. It has also been said that this was from him, upon him be peace, because of the weakness of old age. They said: his age at that time was sixty. It has been said: sixty-five; it has been said: seventy; it has been said: seventy-five; it has been said: eighty; it has been said: more than that. As has passed in the explanation of Surah Al 'Imran.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 4:

﴿He said﴾ is an explanatory clause (jumla mufassira) for "nada" (he called out), and it has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis).

﴿My Lord, indeed my bones have weakened within me﴾. The attribution of weakness (wahn) to the bone is because it is the pillar (imad) of the body and the support (di'am) of the frame; when weakness and slackening afflict it, they afflict the whole. Or it is because it is the hardest and most firmly structured of its parts, and the least affected by ailments, so when it weakens, what lies beyond it is even weaker. Its being mentioned in the singular is intended to refer to the genus (al-jins), which indicates that the weakness encompasses every individual member of it. "Minni" (from me) is connected to a omitted verb and is a circumstantial phrase (hal) of "al-'azm" (the bone). It is also read as (wahina) with a kasra on the ha', and also with a damma. The emphasis of the clause (ta'kid al-jumla) serves to show the utmost concern in establishing its content.

﴿And the head has blazed with grey hair﴾. Peace be upon him compared the grey hair, in its whiteness and brightness, to the flame of fire (shuwaz al-nar), and its spreading through the hair, its pervading it, and its taking hold of it in every direction, to the blazing of fire. Then he expressed this in the mode of metaphor (isti'ara); then he attributed the blazing (ishtial) to the place where the hair grows and springs forth, and expressed it in the mode of specification (tamyiz). He used the absolute "head" (al-ra's) being content with what he restricted the bone by. In it there are of the arts of eloquence and the perfection of forcefulness what is not hidden, since the original was "the grey hair of my head blazed," so he attributed the blazing to the head, as mentioned, to indicate its inclusion of all of it. Its relation to the original is like the relation of "his house blazed with fire" to "fire blazed in his house." It also serves to reinforce its affirmation, first in summary and then in detail. And for the greater magnification of it, it is indefinite (tankir). It is also read with the idgham of the sin into the shin.

﴿And I have never been unsuccessful in my prayer to You, my Lord﴾. That is: I have never been disappointed in my supplication to You at any time during this long life; rather, whenever I called upon You, You answered me. The clause is coordinated with what precedes it, or is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of the speaker, since the meaning is: "and my head blazed with grey hair." This is an appeal (tawassul) by him, peace be upon him, through what had preceded from Him in the answering of every supplication, following the preparation of what calls for mercy and draws compassion, from the advanced age and weakness of condition. For He, exalted is He, after accustoming His servant to answering for a long time, hardly would disappoint him ever, especially at his moment of distress and extreme need. And in both places there is a mention of the attribute of lordship (rububiyya), which indicates the attachment of what is good for the one who is nurtured (al-marbub) together with the attachment to his pronoun, peace be upon him, especially placing it between "kana" and its predicate, to stir the chain of answering by exaggerating in supplication. For this reason it has been said: when a servant wants his supplication to be answered, let him call upon God, exalted is He, by what suits it of His names and attributes.

﴿And indeed I fear my successors (al-mawali)﴾. It is coordinated with His saying, exalted is He: "indeed my bones have weakened within me," its content following upon its content, for the weakening of strength and advanced age are among the beginnings of his fear, peace be upon him, of those who would take charge of his affairs after his death. His successors (mawali) are his paternal cousins, and they were among the worst of the Children of Israel, so he feared that they would not manage his succession well among his community, and would alter their religion for them. And His saying:

﴿From behind me﴾ means: after my death. It is connected to an implied element that the mind is led to, namely: the conduct of the heirs (mawali) after me, or the oppression of the heirs. It has also been read as ﴿كَذَلِكَ﴾ (kadhalika), or with what the word mawali contains of the meaning of guardianship (wilaya), i.e., "I feared those who will take charge of affairs behind me." It is not read as ﴿بِخْفِتُ﴾ (bi-khiftu), because that corrupts the meaning. It has been read as ﴿وَرايَ﴾ (waraya), with the alif shortened and the ya vowelled with a fatha. It has also been read as ﴿خَفَّتِ المَوالِي مِن ورائِي﴾ (khaffati al-mawali min waraya), meaning: they became few and unable to carry out the affairs of religion after me; or, the heirs who were capable of upholding the rites of the religion and the interests of the community became few. This is from khaffa al-qawm, meaning they departed hastily, i.e., they passed on ahead of me, and none remained among them who could be relied upon for support. In that case the adverbial phrase (zarf) is connected to khiftu.

﴿And my wife has been barren﴾ means: she has not borne children since her youth.

﴿So grant me from Yourself﴾: both prepositional phrases (al-jarran) are connected to hab (grant), since their meanings differ. The lam is the complement of it (silah lahu), and min is for the beginning of the limit (ibtida' al-ghaya), used metaphorically. The first is placed first because what it signifies is more important to him. It is also permissible for the second to be connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the object. Ladun is originally an adverb (zarf) meaning the nearest limit of a time, a place, or other entities. Its detailed treatment has passed in the beginning of Surah Al 'Imran. The meaning is: give me from the pure bounty of Your vast favour and Your overwhelming power, by way of originating (al-ikhtira'), not through ordinary causes.

﴿A heir (waliyyan)﴾ means: a child from my own loins. Placing it after the two prepositional phrases shows the complete concern with the gift being granted to him in this wondrous manner, together with the eagerness it creates for the delayed element. When something that should come first is delayed, the soul remains expectant, and upon its arrival it settles there more firmly. Also, because it is a lengthy element with the descriptive phrase following it, placing the two phrases after everything else, or placing them between the qualified noun and its qualifier, is not befitting the eloquence of the noble composition. The fa' (fa') indicates that what follows is consequent upon what precedes, since what he mentioned, upon him be peace, of advanced age, weakness of strength, and his wife's barrenness, necessitates the cutting off of his hope of having a child through ordinary causes, and so he asked for it in the manner that breaks habit. It does not detract from this that there was another motive for turning to the aforementioned supplication, namely his witnessing of the manifest extraordinary events concerning Maryam (peace be upon her), as indicated by the words of the Exalted: ﴿There Zechariah called upon his Lord﴾ ... the verse. The omission of mention of it here relies on its mention there, just as the omission of mention of the prelude to the supplication there is for sufficiency with its mention here. For the sufficiency of what is mentioned in one place over what is left out in another is among the subtleties of revelation (al-nukat al-tanziliyya). And the words of the Exalted:

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 6:**

﴿Who will inherit from me﴾: this is a descriptive clause (ṣifah) modifying *waliyyan* ("an heir"). It has also been read with the jussive, *yarithnī* ("he will inherit me"), and what is conjoined to it, as a response to the supplication (*jawāban li-l-du'ā'*). The meaning is: he will inherit from me in terms of knowledge, religion and prophethood, for the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, do not bequeath wealth. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from; what we leave behind is charity." (p-255) It has also been said: he will inherit from me the *ḥubūrah* (the rank of scholar, *ḥibr*). Zakariyya, upon him be peace, was a *ḥibr*.

﴿and inherit from the family of Ya'qub﴾: it is said *waratha-hu* and *waritha min-hu*, two dialectal forms meaning "he inherited it." The "family" (*āl*) of a man is his close circle, those whose affairs return to him, either by kinship, companionship, or agreement in religion. Zakariyya's wife was the sister of Maryam's mother; that is, he will inherit from them the kingship. It has been said that this Ya'qub is Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim, upon them be blessings and peace. Al-Kalbi and Muqatil said that he is Ya'qub son of Mathan, brother of Imran son of Mathan, of the lineage of Sulayman, upon him be peace, and the family of Ya'qub were the maternal relatives of Yahya son of Zakariyya. Al-Kalbi said: the sons of Mathan were the chiefs and kings of the Children of Israel, and Zakariyya was then the chief of the rabbis. He wanted his son to inherit his scholarly rank and to inherit from the sons of Mathan their kingship.

It has been read as *wa-yarithu wārith āli Ya'qūb* (with *wārith* as an accusative of state), being a circumstantial adjective (ḥāl) from the pronoun hidden in *yarithu*. It has also been read *aw yarithu āla Ya'qūb* with the diminutive (*āl* becoming *uhayl*), which hints at his inheriting, in his childhood, what he would inherit. It has also been read *wārithun min āli Ya'qūb* as the subject of *yarithunī*, in the figurative manner (*ṭarīqat al-tajrīd*), meaning: an heir will inherit through him. It has been said that *min* is partitive (*lil-tab'īḍ*), since not every family of Ya'qub, upon him be peace, were prophets or scholars.

﴿and make him, my Lord, one who is pleasing﴾: *marḍiyyan* means accepted by You in word and deed. The placement of *rabbi* between the two objects of *ijʿal* is for emphasis, showing the intensity of care for what he is asking for.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah (chapter) 19, verse 7:

﴿O Zakariyya﴾, on the understanding that a verb of saying is implied, i.e., Allah the Exalted said: O Zakariyya, ﴿Indeed, We give you good news of a boy whose name is Yahya﴾. However, this was not by Allah addressing him, peace be upon him, directly with this, but through the angel, with Allah the Exalted relating this statement to him, peace be upon him, in the manner of His saying: ﴿Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves...﴾ the verse. Its verification has already passed in Surah Al 'Imran. This is a response to his call, peace be upon him, and a promise to answer his supplication, but not entirely, as is evident from His saying: ﴿So We answered him and gave him Yahya﴾ ... etc. Rather, it is in part, as the divine will, which is founded on profound wisdoms, requires. For the prophets, peace be upon them, although their supplications are answered, are not so in all supplications. Do you not see the supplication of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, on behalf of his father, and the supplication of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he said: "And I asked Him not to make them taste the violence of one another, but He denied me that." It was part of the decree of the Mighty and Exalted that He would grant him Yahya as a prophet who is well-pleasing, and that he would not inherit from him. So his supplication was answered in the first matter but not the second, since he was killed before his father's death, according to what is well known. It was said that he remained for a while after him, and then there is no difficulty at that point. Specifying his name, peace be upon him, is a confirmation of the promise and an honour for him, peace be upon him. In singling him out with it, peace be upon him, as indicated by His saying: ﴿We have not made for him before a namesake (samiyyan)﴾, i.e., a partner in the name, since no one was named Yahya before him, is an increase in honour and an exaltation of him, peace be upon him. For naming with unique names that are distinct from the names of the rest of people is necessarily a mark of distinction for the one named. It was said: samiyyan means a likeness in excellence and perfection, as in His saying: ﴿Do you know of anyone with the same name (samiyyan) as Him?﴾, for those who share a quality are in the position of those who share a name. They said: he, peace be upon him, had no equal in that he never disobeyed Allah the Exalted, never intended a sin at all, was born to an aged old man and a barren old woman, and that he was chaste (ḥaṣūran). Thus this is a summary of what was revealed after him in His saying: ﴿Confirming a word from Allah, and a noble leader, and chaste, and a prophet from among the righteous﴾. The more apparent view is that the name is non-Arabic (a'jami), and if it is Arabic, then it is derived from a verb, like Ya'mar and Ya'ish. It was said: he was named so because the womb of his mother came alive through him, or because the religion of Allah the Exalted came alive through his call.

(p-256) ﴿Qāla﴾ (He said) is a resumptive clause (*istiʾnāf*) answering an implied question, as if it were asked: "What did he (peace be upon him) say at that time?" It is answered: "He said: ﴿Rabbi﴾ (My Lord)." God, the Exalted, addressed him directly, though His address reached him through the intermediary of the angel, in order to intensify the supplication, the intimate prayer, and the earnest devotion (*tabattul*) toward Him, exalted be He. It also guards against the possible misunderstanding that might arise from His speaking to the angel: that God's knowledge of what proceeds from him depends on that intermediary, just as human knowledge of what proceeds from Him, glorified be He, depends on such intermediaries in most circumstances.

﴿Anna yakūnu lī ghulām﴾ (How can I have a boy?). The word ﴿anna﴾ means "how" or "from where." The verb ﴿kāna﴾ may be complete (*tāmma*), in which case ﴿anna﴾ and the ﴿lām﴾ (in ﴿lī﴾) are both connected to it. The fronting of the prepositional phrase before the subject is, as has been noted many times, for the sake of giving attention to what is fronted and creating suspense for what is delayed. The meaning is: "How, or from where, will a boy come into being for me?" It is also permissible for the ﴿lām﴾ to be connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) of ﴿ghulām﴾, since if it were postponed it would be an attribute of it. The meaning would then be: "How will a boy come to be existing for me?" Or the verb may be defective (*nāqiṣa*), with its subject being the apparent noun, and its predicate being either ﴿anna﴾ with ﴿lī﴾ connected to an omitted element, as mentioned, or the predicate itself, with ﴿anna﴾ in the accusative as an adverb of place (*ẓarfiyya*).

﴿Wa-kānat imraʾatī ʿāqiran﴾ (and my wife has been barren) is a circumstantial clause from the speaker's pronoun, with ﴿qad﴾ implied. Likewise, ﴿wa-qad balaghtu mina l-kibari ʿitiyyan﴾ (and I have indeed reached extreme old age) is a circumstantial clause from the same pronoun, emphasizing the improbability following an earlier emphasis. The meaning is: "My wife was barren and did not bear children in her youth or in my youth; how then (will it happen) now that she is an old woman, while I have reached, by reason of advanced age, stiffness and dryness in the joints and bones?" Or: "I have reached, in the stages and degrees of old age, that which is called ʿitiyyan?!"

The word ﴿ʿitiyyan﴾ derives from ʿataa, yaʿtū, and its root is ʿutuww, like quʿūd. The succession of two *ḍammas* and two *wāws* was felt to be heavy, so the *tāʾ* was given a *kasra*. The first *wāw* became a *yāʾ* because it was quiescent and preceded by a *kasra*. Then the second was also changed, since a *wāw* and *yāʾ* came together and the first of them was quiescent. The ʿayn was given a *kasra* to match what followed it. It is also read with a *ḍamma* on the ʿayn.

Perhaps the mention here begins with the state of his wife, in reverse order from what is in Surat Āl ʿImrān, because his own state had already been mentioned within the supplication. What is mentioned here is only that he reached the utmost stages of old age, as a completion of what was mentioned before. In Āl ʿImrān, however, his state had not been mentioned earlier in the supplication, so he mentioned it first before the state of his wife, since hastening to explain the weakness of his own condition is more fitting.

He said this, peace be upon him, although he had already made supplication with it and had strong certainty in God's power, especially after witnessing the signs mentioned in Surat Āl ʿImrān. He said it to magnify God's power, to express wonder at it, and to acknowledge God's favor upon him in this matter, by showing that it was purely from God's grace and bounty, mighty and exalted, even though it is, in itself, among the things customarily deemed impossible, not as a sign of disbelief in it.

It has also been said that he said it so that he would be answered with what he was answered, so that the believers would increase in certainty and the falsifiers would be deterred. It has also been said that this was from him, peace be upon him, as an inquiry about the manner in which it would occur. And it has been said: rather, it was by way of wonder (*istibʿād*), since there were sixty years between the supplication and the good tidings, and he had forgotten his supplication. But this is far-fetched.

(p-257) Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 9:

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), as explained earlier, built on a question arising from what preceded. The *kaf* (ك) in His saying, ﴿Thus your Lord said﴾, is an interposed particle (muqhamah), as in the expression مِثْلُكَ لا يَبْخَلُ ("the like of you does not stint"). Its position (mahall) is either accusative, as an adverbial infinitive (masdar tashbihi) of the second "said" (qala). The word *dhalika* ("thus") refers to its verbal noun, which is the promise mentioned earlier, and not to some other saying to which this is being compared. Its verification has already been discussed in the commentary on His saying: ﴿And thus We made you a justly balanced community﴾.

His saying, ﴿It is easy for Me﴾, is a clause that confirms the aforementioned promise and indicates its fulfilment. It falls within the scope of the first "said", as if it were said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: like that saying of wonder, I have said" — that is, like that promise which breaks the customary order, [it is] easy for Me, specifically, though it may be impossible according to custom. It has also been recited as (وَهُوَ عَلَيَّ هَيِّنٌ) "and He, it is easy for Me," in which case the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to "your Lord," and the *ya'* (ي) is an expression of His pronoun, as you will come to know; or it is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraid). In every case it emphasises and confirms what came before it.

Then the second saying is presented in the mode of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), in keeping with the manner of majesty, so as to show him awe and to instil dread, like the statement of the caliphs: "The Commander of the Faithful draws for you" in place of "I draw". Then it is attributed to the name of the Lord, joined to His pronoun, peace be upon him, as an honour to him and as an indication of the reason for the ruling. For reminding him that the rulings of His lordship (rububiyyah), exalted is He, apply to him, peace be upon him — from bringing him into existence from non-existence, and from directing him through the stages of creation from state to state, gradually, until he reaches the perfection suited to him — removes the root of his peace-be-upon-him sense of the improbability of the promised outcome, and gives him, peace be upon him, the assurance that it will be fulfilled without fail.

Then the reference shifts from the third-person pronoun referring to the Lord to the *ya'* of greatness (ياء العظمة, the first-person singular of majesty), signalling that the basis of its being easy for Him, glorified is He, is His essential power, and not merely His lordship over him, peace be upon him, specifically, and as a preparation for what follows. It has been said that *dhalika* ("thus") refers to something vague which the saying ﴿It is easy for Me﴾ explains, following the manner of His saying: ﴿And We decreed to him that matter: that the root of these would be cut off by morning﴾. This view does not exclude the reading with *wa* (و), and also because the *wa* does not enter between the explainer and the explained.

As for the nominative reading (الرَّفْع), it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and *dhalika* refers to what preceded of His promise, meaning: "He, Mighty and Exalted, said: the matter is as I promised, and it will certainly occur." His saying, ﴿Your Lord said﴾ ... etc., is a resumptive clause confirming its content. The reported clause in the second reading is conjoined to the first reported clause, or is a circumstantial clause (hal) of the pronoun hidden in the preposition-and-object phrase. In either case, placing "said" between the two indicates added attention to each of them. The discussion concerning the attribution of the saying to the Lord, and then the shift to the first-person speaking, is like what passed a moment ago.

It has also been said that *dhalika* refers to what Zakariyya, peace be upon him, had said, meaning: "He, exalted is He, said: the matter is as you have said," confirming him in what he had related of the state, contrary to childbirth, in himself and in his wife. His saying, ﴿Your Lord said﴾ ... etc., is a resumptive clause driven to remove his sense of improbability after affirming it, meaning: "He, exalted is He, though it is improbable in itself, said: it is easy for Me." The second reading is more suited to conveying this meaning, given that the *wa* is conjunctive. As for making it circumstantial (lil-hal), that disturbs the soundness of the meaning, because its outcome would be to affirm its difficulty while it is easy for Him, exalted is He, whereas the intended purpose is to show its ease for Him, glorified is He, despite its difficulty in itself.

His saying, ﴿And I created you before, when you were nothing﴾, is a resumptive clause confirming what precedes it. What is meant by it is the beginning of the creation of humankind, which occurs immediately after pure non-existence, and not what came after that by the customary process of procreation. And the reason this is not attributed to Adam, peace be upon him, who was created from non-existence in truth, by saying: "And I created your father or Adam before, when he was nothing," although that would suffice to remove the sense of improbability through analogy of the condition of what was announced to the condition of him, peace be upon him, to strengthen the argument by it and to clarify the method of analogy, is because it draws attention to the fact that every individual of humankind has a share in his creation, peace be upon him, from non-existence. For his unique nature was not confined to himself, but was a model containing within it the natural disposition of all the individuals of the species, in a general (ijmali) containment that entails the operation of its effects upon all. Thus his origination, peace be upon him, in that manner was an origination of every one of his descendants likewise. And since his creation, peace be upon him, in this pattern which extends to all individuals of his progeny was more wondrous than if that were confined to himself, as is the understanding from attributing the aforementioned creation to him, and more indicative of the greatness of His power, exalted is He, and the perfection of His knowledge and wisdom. And Zakariyya's non-existence at that time was more evident to him and clearer. And his state was more deserving of being a standard for the state of what he was given tidings of, to which the aforementioned creation was attributed, just as creation and shaping were attributed to the addressees in His saying: ﴿And We created you, then fashioned you﴾, to render the station of favour its due. So it is as if it were said: "And I created you before, within the course of Adam's creation, and you were not then anything at all, but pure non-existence and sheer negation." This is the point. As for interpreting "thing" as "that which counts", meaning "you were not a thing that counts", this is rejected by the context and contradicted by the structure of the speech.

It has been recited as (خَلَقْناكَ) "We created you."

﴿He said, "My Lord, appoint for me a sign."﴾ That is, a sign that makes me certain of the granting of what was promised and of the occurrence of the pregnancy. This request was not made by him, peace be upon him, to confirm and establish the glad tidings, as has been said. That would not befit the station of prophethood (*risalah*, the office of messenger), and it was only to make known the time of conception, since the glad tidings did not specify it. That is a hidden matter that cannot be known except by revelation, so he wished that Allah, exalted is He, would inform him of it, so that he might receive that manifest blessing with gratitude from the moment it occurred, and not delay it until it became apparent in the usual way. The commentary on Surat Al 'Imran has already pointed out that this request should have come some time after the glad tidings, because it is reported that Yahya was six months or three years older than Isa, peace be upon them both. There is no doubt that Zakariyya's supplication, peace be upon him, was made while Maryam was still a child, because of the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿There Zakariyya called upon his Lord﴾, and she only bore Isa, peace be upon him, when she was ten or thirteen years old.

The verb *ja'ala* (to make, appoint) here is *ibda'i* (creative, bringing into being), and the *lam* (for) is connected to it. Its placement before the direct object (*mafúl bihi*, object) is because of the emphasis on what is placed first and the arousing of curiosity for what comes later. Alternatively, the *lam* is connected to a deleted element that functions as a *hal* (circumstantial accusative) of *ayah*, since if it came after it, it would be a *sifah* (qualifier) of it. It has also been said that *ja'ala* means "to make (someone) become," which requires two objects. Then either *ayah* is the first object and the prepositional phrase is the second, or *ayah* is the second and the prepositional phrase is the first. The prepositional phrase is placed first because there is no justification for *ayah* to be a *mubtada'* (subject) when the sentence is analysed into subject and predicate, except by placing the adverbial phrase first. Thus their status does not change after the entry of the *nasikh* (the abrogating particle, which alters the status of the nominal sentence).

﴿He said, "Your sign is that you will not speak to people"﴾, that is, that you will not be able to speak to them in human speech, although you will be able to remember and glorify God.

﴿for three nights﴾, together with their days, as is stated explicitly in Surat Al 'Imran.

﴿while sound﴾: *sawiyyan* is a *hal* (circumstantial accusative) of the subject of *tukallima* (you speak). It indicates that the absence of speech occurs by compulsion and not by choice. That is, you will be prevented from speech, so you will not be able to use it, while you are, apart from the creation, sound in your limbs, with no trace of muteness or dumbness in you.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 11:

﴿So he came out to his people from the sanctuary (miḥrāb)﴾. That is: from the place of prayer (muṣallā), or from the upper chamber (ghurfa). They had been behind the miḥrāb, waiting for him, expecting that the door would be opened for them so they could enter and pray. Then he came out to them with his complexion changed, and they disapproved of him and said: "What is wrong with you?"

﴿So he gestured to them﴾. That is: he signaled to them, based on His saying, Exalted is He: "except by gesture (ramz)." It was also said: he wrote on the ground. As for "an" in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿that glorify [Him]﴾, it is either an explanatory particle for "awḥā" (he gestured), or a verbal particle (maṣdariyya). The meaning is: "Pray," or "by praying."

﴿Morning and evening﴾. These are two adverbs of time for the glorification (tasbīḥ). From Abu al-'Aliya: the intended meaning of the two is the Fajr prayer and the 'Asr prayer. Or: glorify your Lord at the two ends of the day. Perhaps he had been commanded to glorify (Him) out of gratitude, and to command his people to do the same.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 12:

﴿O Yahya﴾. This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), with many sentences omitted before it in haste to report the fulfilment of the generous promise; that is, "We said: O Yahya" (p-259), ﴿take the Book﴾, meaning the Torah, ﴿with strength﴾, that is, with earnestness and with seeking strength through divine success (tawfiq).

﴿And We gave him judgment while still a child﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "The judgment (al-hukm) is prophethood; he was made a prophet when he was three years old." It was also said: the judgment is wisdom (al-hikmah), the understanding of the Torah, and comprehension of the religion (al-fiqh fi al-din). It is narrated that the children invited him to play, and he said: "We were not created for play."

and affection from Us, and purity. He was God-fearing (taqiyy),

"And tenderness (hanan) from Us" is conjoined with the judgment (al-hukm) (mentioned in the preceding verse), and its tanwin (indefinite ending) is for magnification (li-l-tafkhim). It means compassion and longing (al-tahannun wa-l-ishtiyaq). The "min" (from) is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a qualifier of it, emphasizing what the tanwin conveys of grandeur in its essential nature through grandeur by way of attribution. That is: "And We gave him a great mercy from Our presence," or "mercy in his heart and compassion toward his parents and others."

"And purity (zakah)": that is, purity from sins; or charity (sadaqah) which We gave on his behalf to his parents; or We enabled him to show charity to people.

"And he was God-fearing (taqiyy)": obedient, keeping far away from acts of disobedience.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 14:**

﴿And dutiful to his parents﴾ is conjoined to "pious" (taqiyyan), meaning: dutiful towards them, gentle towards them, and beneficent to them.

﴿And he was not arrogant (jabbaran) or disobedient (asiyyan)﴾: haughty, undutiful to his parents; or disobedient to his Lord.

[Peace be upon him] from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿on the day he was born﴾ from being touched by Satan in the manner in which Satan touches the children of Adam.

﴿And on the day he dies﴾ from the punishment of the grave, ﴿and on the day he is raised alive﴾ from the terror of the Resurrection and the punishment of the Fire.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on Surah 19, Verse 16:**

﴿And mention in the Book﴾ is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*, a sentence begun afresh and not grammatically dependent on what precedes it). It is addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), who was commanded to relate the story of Maryam immediately after the story of Zakariyya, because of the very close connection between them. By "the Book" is meant the blessed surah, not the Qur'an as a whole. This is because it is the surah that opens with the story of Zakariyya, which entails the mention of her story and the stories of the prophets mentioned in it. That is, [it means]: "and mention to the people."

﴿Maryam﴾: that is, her account, for mention does not attach to persons themselves. His, may He be exalted, saying ﴿when she withdrew﴾ is an adverbial clause (*zarf*) modifying that omitted noun (her account). However, this does not mean that what is commanded is mentioning her withdrawal only at the moment of withdrawing, but rather everything that is conjoined to it. What is related after it, by way of resumption, falls within the scope of the adverbial clause and completes the account. It has also been said that it is an inclusion apposition (*badal al-ishtimal*, an apposition in which the second term is related to the first by being contained in it) for Maryam, on the understanding that what is meant by her is her account, since adverbial clauses contain what is in them. It has also been said that it is a comprehensive apposition (*badal al-kull*, in which the second term covers the whole of the first), on the understanding that what is meant by the adverbial clause is what occurred in it. It has also been said that *idh* (﴿when﴾) here carries the meaning of the verbal particle *an* (that), as in your saying, "I honoured you because you did not honour me," meaning "because you did not honour me." In that case it is unquestionably an inclusion apposition.

His, may He be exalted, saying ﴿from her people﴾ is connected to *intabadhat* (she withdrew). His saying ﴿a place toward the east﴾ is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*, a noun giving the reason for the action) by virtue of what is implied in it of the meaning of "coming" (*ityan*), which follows it in existence and in consideration, and which operates on the basic meaning of the prepositional phrase. This is the secret of placing it after the prepositional phrase. The meaning is: she separated herself from them, withdrew from them, and went to a place toward the east of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), or of her house, in order to be alone there for worship. It has also been said that she sat facing east in order to wash from menstruation, screened by a wall or by something that covered her. This is His, may He be exalted, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 17:

﴿So she took a screen apart from them﴾ Her place had been the mosque; when she menstruated she would move to the house of her maternal aunt, and when she became pure she would return to the mosque. Then, while she was in her bathing place (p-260), the angel, upon him be peace, came to her in the form of a beardless young man of human appearance, with a handsome face and curly hair. This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We sent to her Our Spirit﴾, that is, Jibril, upon him be peace. He was referred to thus to give the station its due. It has also been recited with a fatha on the rā' (Rūḥanā), because he was the means of the spirit (rūḥ) of the servants being in him, which is the provision of those brought near, in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But if he is of those brought near, then [there is] rest and bounty﴾.

﴿So he appeared to her as a well-proportioned man﴾: of sound creation, complete in structure, lacking none of the fine attributes of humanity. It was said that he appeared in the guise of a relative of hers named Yusuf, one of the servants of Bayt al-Maqdis, so that she would be at ease with his speech and would receive from him what he conveyed to her of the words of Allah, for had he appeared to her in angelic form she would have fled from him and been unable to converse with him. As for what has been said, that this was to stir up her desire so that her sperm would descend into her womb, then, besides its incompatibility with the context of demonstrating the signs of supernatural power beyond custom, His saying, exalted is He, refutes it:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 18:

﴿She said: "Indeed I seek refuge in the Most Merciful from you."﴾ Her saying this is a trustworthy testimony that no trace of inclination toward him had occurred to her mind, let alone what was mentioned of the state that follows from the utmost degree of inclination and desire. Yes, his appearing to her in that surpassing beauty and gleaming loveliness was for the sake of testing her and probing her chastity. In fact, there appeared from her such piety (wara') and modesty (iffah) that there is no further limit beyond it. Her mention of Him, the Exalted, by the title of "the Most Merciful" serves to intensify her seeking refuge in Him, the Exalted, and to draw forth the effects of the special mercy, which is protection (ismah) from what had overtaken her.

And His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿If you are God-fearing﴾ means: you who fear God, the Exalted, and are mindful of seeking refuge in Him. The response of the conditional is omitted, relying confidently on the context indicating it, that is: "then I am seeking refuge in Him," or "then you will take refuge in my seeking refuge," or "then do not approach me."

Abu al-Su'ud, Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, on surah 19, verse 19:

﴿He said, "I am only the messenger of your Lord"﴾ meaning, peace be upon him: I am not one from whom what you imagined of evil is to be expected. Rather, I am only the messenger of your Lord, whom you sought refuge in.

﴿to give you a pure boy﴾ i.e., so that I may be the cause of his being given to you by breathing into the garment. It is also possible that this is a quotation of His, exalted is He, saying: "I am only the messenger of your Lord." This is supported by the reading with the yā' (لأهَبَ with the first person singular "I"), and by the mention of the title "Lord" (Rabb) together with its being attributed to her pronoun, to honour her, to console her, and to indicate the reason for the ruling, for giving her a boy is among the rulings of her upbringing. In some codices it reads: "my Lord commanded me that I give you a boy."

﴿pure﴾ free from sins, or growing upon goodness, i.e., progressing from one age to another upon goodness and righteousness.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 20:

﴿She said: "How can I have a boy,﴾ as you have described, ﴿when no man has touched me,﴾ i.e., while the situation is that no man has approached me in marriage (nikah). It is said "basharun" (man) for emphasis in declaring her purity from the beginnings of childbearing. ﴿Nor have I been unchaste (baghiyyan).﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon "lam yamsasni" and is included with it in the sense of the circumstantial clause (hal), expressing the meaning of "touch," which is a metaphor for intercourse in marriage. That is: nor was I an adulteress seeking men. The word "baghiyyan" is on the pattern fa'ul in the sense of the active participle (fa'il); its original form is baghawiyy. The waw was assimilated after being changed into a yaʾ, into the yaʾ, and the ghayn was given a kasra for the yaʾ. It is also said: it is fa'il in the sense of the active participle, for otherwise it would have been said baghuww, just as it is said: fulanun nahuwwun ʿani al-munkar (so-and-so is one who forbids evil strongly). The taʾ marbutah was not attached to it because it is of the class of relative adjectives (nisba), like ṭāliq. Or it is in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ul), meaning: men seek her for fornication with her.﴾

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 21:

﴿Said﴾, i.e., the angel, confirming his statement and affirming it.

﴿Thus﴾, i.e., the matter is as I told you. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Your Lord said﴾ ... etc., is a resumptive clause (isti'naf) confirming it, meaning: your Lord, who sent me to you, said.

﴿It is﴾, i.e., what I mentioned to you of the gift of a boy without any human ever touching you at all, ﴿for Me﴾ specifically ﴿easy﴾. Although it is ordinarily impossible, it is easy for Me, because I do not need causes or intermediaries. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and that We may make him a sign for the people﴾ is either a reason ('illah) for a suppressed causative clause, meaning: and that We may make the granting of the boy a sign for them and a proof by which they infer the perfection of Our power, We do this. Or it is coordinated (ma'tuf) with another suppressed reason, meaning: that We may demonstrate by it the greatness of Our power, and that We may make him a sign ... etc. The waw according to the first view is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah), and the shift to the plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah) is to manifest the perfection of majesty.

﴿And a mercy﴾, a great mercy existing ﴿from Us﴾ toward them, by which they are guided through his guidance and seek right direction through his instruction.

﴿And it was﴾ that ﴿a matter decreed﴾, settled, its determination having been attached to by Our eternal decree, or it was decreed and inscribed on the Preserved Tablet, so it must certainly come to pass for you without fail. Or it was a real matter, that it be decreed and done, because it includes wise purposes of great consequence.

**﴿So she conceived him﴾**, by Gabriel (Jibril, upon him be peace) blowing into her shift, so the breath entered her womb. It was said that he lifted her shift and blew into her neckline (*jayb*), and she conceived. It was also said that he blew from a distance, the wind reached her, and she conceived at once. It was also said that the breath was in her mouth. The period of her pregnancy was seven months. It was said to be eight months. No child born after eight months has survived except him. It was said to be nine months, and it was said three hours, and it was said one hour. Just as she conceived, she gave birth to him. She was thirteen years old at that time, and it was said ten years. She had menstruated twice.

**﴿Then she withdrew with him﴾**, that is, she withdrew, while he was in her womb, as in the verse of poetry:

*"They trample with us the skulls and the nurayb"*

Here the prepositional phrase *bihi* (with him) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*, circumstantial qualifier), meaning: "she withdrew while being joined with him."

**﴿to a remote place﴾**, far from her people, behind the mountain. It was said: the farthest part of the house. This is the more fitting view, given the short duration of the pregnancy.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 23:**

﴿So the pains of childbirth drove her﴾ i.e., ﴿fa- alja'aha﴾ (compelled her). It is originally derived from *jā'a* (to come), but it is not used in any other sense, like *ātā* in *a'twā* (to give). It was also read as *al-mikhāḍu* with a kasra on the *mīm*. Both are the verbal noun of *makhidat al-mar'ah* (the woman experienced labor pains), when the child moves in her womb in preparation for emergence.

﴿to the trunk of the palm tree﴾ so that she might conceal herself with it and lean on it at the time of birth. It is what lies between the root and the branch. It was a dry palm with no top and no greenery, and the time was winter. The definite article is either for the genus (*li-l-jins*) or for a specific reference (*li-l-'ahd*), if there was no other palm tree there. It was well known among the people, and perhaps God inspired her to this so that He would show her among His signs what would calm her fright and feed her the fresh dates (*rutab*), which is the postpartum nourishment suitable for her.

﴿She said: "Would that I had died﴾ with a kasra on the *mīm* from *māta yamātu* like *khiftu*; it was also read with a damma on the *mīm* from *māta yamūtu*.

﴿before this﴾ i.e., before this time in which she encountered what she encountered. She said this although she knew what had passed between her and Gabriel (peace be upon him) of the noble promise, out of shame before people and fear of their blame; or out of caution lest the people fall into sin by what they would say about it; or following the custom of the righteous when a matter becomes severe for them, as it is narrated from ʿUmar (may God be pleased with him) that he took a straw from the ground and said: "Would that I were this straw and had been nothing." And from Bilal that he said: "Would that his mother had not borne Bilal."

﴿and I had been a thing forgotten﴾ i.e., a trivial thing whose nature is to be forgotten and not regarded at all. It was also read with a kasra. It is said: they are two dialects for this, like *al-watr* and *al-witr*. It is said: with a kasra it is a noun for what is forgotten, like *al-niqḍ* is a noun for what is broken down; and with a fatha it is a verbal noun used as the passive participle for emphasis. It was also read with both, hamzated, from *nasa'tu al-laban* when you pour water onto it so it becomes diluted in it; and it was read *nasan* like *'asan*.

﴿utterly forgotten﴾ that does not come to the mind of anyone among the people; it is an adjective in intensive form. It was also read with a kasra on the *mīm*, following the *sīn*.

﴿So he called to her﴾, that is, Gabriel, peace be upon him, ﴿from beneath her﴾. It was said that he used to receive the child. It was also said that "from beneath her" means from a place lower than her, beneath the hillock. It was said that it means from beneath the palm tree. It was said that Jesus, peace be upon him, called to her.

It was read as "fakhatabaha man tahtaha" with a fatḥa on the mīm.

﴿Do not grieve﴾, that is, do not grieve. The "an" (أنْ) here is *mufassirah* (explanatory). Or it is *maṣdariyyah* (verbal, introducing a verbal clause), with the preposition removed: "that you should not grieve."

﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you﴾, that is, in a place lower than you. It was said: "beneath your command," so that if you command it to flow, it flows, and if you command it to stop, it stops.

﴿a stream﴾, that is, a small river, as was narrated in a report traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Gabriel, peace be upon him, struck the earth with his foot, and a spring of sweet water appeared, and it flowed as a rivulet. It was said that Jesus, peace be upon him, did this. It was also said that there was a dry river there, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, caused water to flow in it at that time, just as He did the same with the palm tree, for it was a dry palm with no crown, no leaves, let alone fruit. It was winter, so Allah then gave it a crown, fronds, and fruit. It was also said that there was flowing water there. The first view is the one consistent with the context of showing the manifestation of extraordinary signs, and it is what is immediately understood from the noble wording.

It was also said: *sariyyan* means a noble master,高 in rank and majestic, and this is Jesus, peace be upon him. In that case the *tanwīn* (nunation) is for magnification, and the clause is a reason for the negation of grief implied by the prohibition against it. The mention of the title "Lord" together with its attachment to her pronoun serves to honour her, to emphasise the reason, and to complete the consolation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 25:

﴿And shake﴾ Hazz (shaking) of a thing is moving it toward opposite directions with a vigorous, successive motion. What is meant here is that which is done by way of pulling and pushing, owing to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿towards you﴾, i.e., towards your direction. The "ba'" (bi, "with") in His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿by the trunk of the palm tree﴾ is a particle of emphasis, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not throw yourselves with your own hands﴾ ... etc. Al-Farra' said: the Arabs say hazzahu and hazza bihi, and akhadha al-khitam and akhadha bil-khitam (both meaning "he took the halter"). Or it is for attaching the action to what follows it, i.e., perform the shaking of its trunk, or shake the dates by shaking it. It has also been said: it is connected to an omitted element that occurs as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the object of the shaking, i.e., shake towards yourself the fresh dates while they are [still] by its trunk.

﴿will drop﴾ i.e., the palm tree will drop.

﴿upon you﴾ a continuous dropping in accordance with the continuity of the shaking. It is read as (tusqit) and (yusqit) from the causative iqa' with ta' and ya', and as (tatasaqat) with both ta's made apparent, and (tasaqat) with the second removed, and (tassaqat) with its assimilation into the sin, and (yassaqat) with ya' likewise. It is also read (tasquth) and (yasquth) from suquth (falling), on the basis that the ta' in all of them refers to the palm tree and the ya' to the trunk. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿fresh dates﴾ is, according to the three readings, the object in the first reading, and in the remaining six it is a specification (tamyiz). His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ripe﴾ is an attribute of it, namely that which is picked before it dries, on the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, i.e., fresh dates that are harvestable, meaning suitable for picking. It has also been said: in the sense of fa'il, i.e., fresh, good. It is also read (jinyyan) with a kasra on the jim, for the sake of harmony.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 26:

﴿So eat and drink﴾ (p-263). That is, the fresh dates and the water of the stream (sarriyy). Or, from the dates and their juice.

﴿And be comforted in eye﴾, and be content in spirit, and cast off from yourself whatever has grieved and troubled you. He, exalted is He, has cleared your sanctuary of what had stirred in the hearts of those who worship through ordinary, customary rules, by showing them, from the elemental simples and the plant compounds, what breaks the natural habits of creation, and by guiding them to recognise the true nature of your affair. It was also read: (wa-qirri) with a kasra on the qaf, and this is the dialect of Najd. Its derivation is from qarar (settling), for when the eye sees what gladdens the soul, it settles upon it and turns away from looking at anything else. Or it is from qarr (coolness), for the tear of joy is cool and the tear of sorrow is hot. Hence one says qurrat al-'ayn (coolness of the eye) and sukhnat al-'ayn (heat of the eye), for the beloved and for the hated.

﴿If you see any human being﴾, that is, any human, whoever he may be. It was also read: (tara'inna), according to the dialect of one who says labba'tu bil-hajj (I answered the call of the pilgrimage, with the hamza). This is because the hamza and the ya are mutually interchangeable (ta'akhi, interchange).

﴿then say﴾ to him, if he questions you:

﴿I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾, that is, a silence, and it was read thus; or a fast (siyam), and their fasting was by keeping silent.

﴿so I will not speak today to any human being﴾, that is, after I have informed you of my vow. Rather, I speak with the angels and I converse with my Lord. It was said that she was commanded to inform them of her vow by gesture, and this is the more apparent view. Al-Farra' said: The Arabs call everything that reaches a person as speech, by whatever means it reaches him, so long as it is not emphasised by the verbal noun (masdar). When it is emphasised, it is nothing but actual speech. She was commanded to do this only because she disliked arguing with the foolish and trading words with them, and because the speech of 'Isa (peace be upon him) suffices, for it is a decisive text in cutting off criticism.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 27:

﴿Then she brought him to her people, carrying him.﴾ That is: she came to them with her child, returning to them after she had become pure from her condition (lit. "from herself").

﴿Carrying him﴾ means: bearing him (in her arms).

﴿They said﴾ rebuking her: ﴿O Maryam, you have certainly come with﴾ meaning: you have done.

﴿Something monstrous (shay'an fariyyan)﴾ meaning: something great and strange, unprecedented and abhorrent, from fara al-jild (farā al-jild), i.e., he cut the hide, or: you have come with an amazing coming. He expressed it with "a thing" (shay') in order to affirm the sense of astonishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 28:

﴿O sister of Harun﴾ This is a resumption (istinaf) serving to renew the expression and to emphasise the rebuke. By it they meant Harun, the Prophet (ﷺ) [i.e., Aaron, brother of Moses], and she was among the descendants of one who had been of his generation of brothers (ṭabaqat al-ukhuwwa). It is also said that she was of his lineage, and that between them there were a thousand years. It is also said that Harun was a righteous man, or a wicked one, who was in their time, and they likened her to him, meaning: you were among us like him in righteousness; or they reviled her with him.

﴿Your father was not a man of evil, nor was your mother an unchaste woman﴾ This is an affirmation that what she brought was a monstrous and abominable thing (fariyyan munkaran), and an alert that committing indecencies on the part of the children of the righteous is more shameful.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 29:

﴿So she pointed to him﴾, that is, to Jesus, peace be upon him, that they should speak to him. The apparent meaning is that she then made clear her vow, and that she was far removed from conversing with people, as she had been commanded. In this there is an indication that what she was commanded to do was to make her vow clear by gesture, not by speech, and combining the two is something unheard of.

﴿They said﴾, rejecting her reply, ﴿How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?﴾ For we have not known in the past of a child being spoken to by a sensible person. It has been said that the phrase "kāna" (was) is used to place the content of the sentence in an indefinite past time that suits both the near and the distant, and here it refers only to the near, by evidence that it is brought for the sake of wonder. It has also been said that "kāna" is superfluous. The adverbial phrase "fi al-mahd" is a complement of "man" (who), and "ṣabiyyan" (a child) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun hidden within it. Or "kāna" is complete (tāmmah), or it is continuous (dā'imah), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah was ever Knowing and Wise﴾.

(p-264) ﴿Qāla﴾ (He said) is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf) answering a question that arises from the context of the noble discourse, as if it were said: "What happened after that?" So it was said: ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Indī ʿabdu Allāh﴾ ("Indeed, I am the servant of Allah"). Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made him speak thus, the most eloquent of those who speak, to establish the truth and to refute those who claim his lordship (rubūbiyyah). It was said that the one who caused ʿĪsā to speak was Zakariyyā, peace and blessings be upon them both. It is related from al-Suddī, may Allah be pleased with him, that when she (Maryam) pointed to him, they became angry and said: "Her mockery of us is more grievous to us than what she has done." It is also narrated that he, peace be upon him, was nursing, and when he heard that, he stopped nursing, turned his face toward them, leaned on his left side, pointed to them with his index finger, and said what he said... etc. It was also said: he spoke these words and then did not speak again until he reached the stage at which children speak.

﴿Ātānīya al-Kitāb﴾ (He has given me the Book), i.e., the Injīl (Gospel), ﴿wa-jaʿalanī nabiyyan﴾ (and made me a prophet).

﴿And He has made me﴾ blessed in spite of that, a source of benefit, and a teacher of goodness. The use of the past tense for the three verbs is either by consideration of what has preceded in the inevitable decree (al-qada' al-mahtum), or by treating what is about to happen as already certainly having happened. It has also been said: Allah perfected his intellect and made him a prophet while still a child.

﴿Wherever I may be﴾, meaning: wherever I am.

﴿And He has enjoined upon me prayer﴾, meaning: He commanded me to perform it as an emphatic command.

﴿And zakah (obligatory almsgiving)﴾: the zakah of wealth, if I come to possess it, or the purification of the soul from vices.

﴿As long as I remain alive﴾, in this world.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 32:

﴿And dutiful toward my mother﴾ is coordinated with "blessed" (mubarakan), meaning: He made me dutiful toward her. It is also read with a kasra (wa-birri bi-wālidatī), which is either a verbal noun (masdar) described by it for emphasis (mubalaghah), or is governed by an implied verb indicated by "He has enjoined upon me" (awsani), meaning: "and He has made it incumbent upon me to be dutiful (barran)." This reading is supported by the reading with a kasra and a genitive case, coordinated with "prayer" and "zakat." The indefiniteness of "barran" is for magnification (tafkhim).

﴿And He has not made me a tyrant (jabbaran), wretched (shaqiyyan)﴾: obstinate (ʿanidan) toward God, Exalted is He, owing to the extremity of his arrogance.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 33:

﴿And peace is upon me the day I was born, and the day I die, and the day I am raised up alive.﴾ This is as it is for Yahya (upon him be peace), namely that the definite article (al-ta'rif) is for reference to a known thing (li-al-'ahd). The more apparent view is that it is for the category (li-al-jins), and it carries an allusive implication of cursing his enemies (al-ta'ridh bi-al-la'n 'ala a'da'ihi). For the affirmation of the category of peace (jins al-salam) for himself is an allusion (ta'ridh) to the affirmation of its opposite for his opponents, as in the Most High's saying: ﴿And peace is upon those who follow the guidance﴾, for it is an allusion that punishment is upon those who deny and turn away.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 34:

﴿That﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the one whose glorious attributes have been detailed, and the sense of distance in it indicates the exaltedness of his rank, the remoteness of his station, and his distinction from others through those praiseworthy virtues, and it places him in the position of something present and perceptible: ﴿Isa, son of Maryam﴾, not what the Christians describe. This is a refutation of them regarding what they claim, in the most eloquent manner and with a demonstrative method (minhaj burhani), since it describes him with the opposites of what they ascribe to him.

﴿the word of truth﴾, with the accusative (bi-l-nasb, ﴿قَوْلَ﴾), on the basis that it is an emphatic verbal noun (masdar mu'akkid, an absolute object used for emphasis) for ﴿He said, "Indeed I am the servant of Allah..."﴾, etc. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is Isa, son of Maryam﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh, a clause inserted between statements) that establishes the content of what precedes it. It was also recited with the nominative (bi-l-raf'), ﴿قَوْلُ﴾, on the basis that it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is the word of truth about which there is no doubt. The construction is an explicative genitive (idafa lil-bayan), and the pronoun refers either to the preceding speech or to the complete account of the story. It has also been said that it is an attribute of Isa, or an appositive to him, or a second predicate. (p-265) Its meaning is: the Word of Allah. It was also recited as ﴿qal al-haqq﴾ ("the Truth said") and ﴿qawl al-haqq﴾, since qawl and qal have the same meaning.

﴿about which they dispute﴾, meaning: they doubt or they quarrel. So the Jews say: he is a sorcerer, and the Christians say: he is the son of Allah. It was also recited with the second-person address (ta' al-khitab), ﴿تَمْتَرُونَ﴾ ("you dispute").

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 35:

﴿It is not for Allah﴾ i.e., it is not proper for Him, nor befitting for Him, the Exalted.

﴿to take to Himself a son; glory be to Him!﴾ This is a refutation of the Christians and a declaration of the transcendence of the Exalted above what they have slandered Him with. The Exalted's words: ﴿When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾ are a rebuke to them, by explaining that the way of the Exalted, when He decrees any matter among matters, is that He attaches His will to it, so it comes to be at that moment without delay. Since this is His way, how could it be imagined that He would have a son?! It was also read: (fayakūna) with a fatḥah, as a response (jawab) to the command. The Exalted's words:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 36:

﴿And indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him.﴾ This is part of the speech of Jesus, peace be upon him. It has been said: it is a conjunction (ʿatf) with his saying, "Indeed I am the servant of Allah," falling under the scope of the speech (al-qawl). It has also been read without the waw, and it has been read with a fatha on the hamza, with the lam elided, meaning: "and because He, exalted is He, is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the mosques are for Allah, so do not invoke anyone alongside Allah.﴾ It has also been said that it is coordinated (maʿtuf) with the prayer (al-ṣalah).

﴿This﴾, i.e., that which I have mentioned of tawhid (monotheism).

﴿is a straight path﴾ whose traveller does not go astray. And the "fa'" (fa, "so") in His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 37:

﴿So the factions differed among themselves﴾ This is for the sake of arranging what follows upon what precedes, as a warning about the evil of their conduct, in that they made what should have produced agreement the source of disagreement. For although the statements of Jesus, peace be upon him, which have been related, are definitive texts that he is God's servant and His messenger, the Jews and the Christians differed, some by deficiency and some by excess, or the Christians split into sects. The Nestorians said: "He is the son of God." The Jacobites said: "He is God who descended to the earth, then ascended to the heavens, exalted be God far above that with a great exaltation." The Melkites said: "He is the servant of God and His prophet."

﴿Woe, then, to those who disbelieve﴾ They are the ones who differed. He expressed them by the relative pronoun to signify that they all disbelieved, and to indicate the cause of the ruling.

﴿from the witnessing of a momentous day﴾ That is: from the witnessing of a day of great terror, reckoning, and recompense, which is the Day of Resurrection. Or: from the time of its witnessing, or from the place of witnessing in it, or from the testimony of that day against them, which is that the angels, the prophets, peace be upon them, their tongues, their ears, their hands, their feet, and the rest of their limbs will testify against them to their disbelief and transgression. Or: from the time of testimony, or from its place. It has also been said: it refers to what they bore witness to concerning Jesus and his mother, peace be upon them both.

﴿Listen to them and see them!﴾ This is an expression of wonder at how keen their hearing and sight will be on that day. Its meaning is that their hearing and their sight [will be...]

﴿The Day they come to Us﴾ for reckoning and recompense, that is, the Day of Resurrection. It is fitting that they be marvelled at, after having been deaf and blind in the world. Or it is a threat of what they will hear and see on that day. It was also said that he was commanded to make them hear and see the promises of that day and what will befall them in it. According to the first view, the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa-al-majrur) is in the nominative position (mawdi' al-raf'), and according to the second view, it is in the accusative position (hayyiz al-nasb).

﴿But the wrongdoers today﴾ that is, in the world (p-266) ﴿are in clear error﴾ whose extent cannot be grasped, since they completely neglected listening and looking. The placement of "the wrongdoers" (al-zalimun) in the position of a pronoun serves to indicate that they are wrongdoers to their own selves in this respect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 39:

﴿And warn them of the Day of Regret﴾ That is: the Day when all people will feel regret, the evildoer over his evildoing, and the good-doer over the scarcity of his good deeds.

﴿When the matter has been decided﴾ That is: the reckoning has been concluded, and the two groups have been separated, one to Paradise and the other to the Fire. It has been related that the Prophet ﷺ was asked about this and said: "When death is brought in the form of a white-speckled ram, and the two groups are looking on, a caller will call out: 'O people of Paradise, eternity, there is no death! O people of the Fire, eternity, there is no death!' So the people of Paradise will increase in joy upon joy, and the people of the Fire in grief upon grief." And "idh" is either a substitute for "Day of Regret," or an adverbial complement of "regret" (al-hasrah), for the verbal noun preceded by the definite article ("al-") governs an explicit object according to some grammarians, so how much more so an adverbial complement? ﴿While they are heedless﴾ That is: heedless of what will be done to them in the Hereafter.

﴿And they do not believe﴾ These are two circumstantial clauses (jumlatan haliyyatan) relating to the implied pronoun in His statement, exalted is He, "in manifest error" (fi dalal mubin); that is: they are settled in that state. Their being in those two states, and what lies between them, constitutes a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh). Alternatively, they are a circumstantial complement of the object of "warn them," meaning: warn them while they are heedless and do not believe. In that case the circumstantial phrase carries the sense of causation (ta'lil).

﴿Indeed, We shall inherit the earth and whoever is upon it﴾. No one will remain upon it other than Us, and there will be no dominion or king for them upon it. Or it means: We shall cause the earth and whoever is upon it to perish through annihilation and destruction, just as an heir takes back his inheritance.

﴿And to Us they will be returned﴾. That is, they will be sent back for recompense, not to anything else, whether independently or jointly.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 41:**

﴿And mention﴾ is coordinated with "warn them" (anzir-hum).

﴿in the Book﴾ i.e., in the surah, or in the Qur'an.

﴿Abraham﴾ i.e., recite to the people his story and convey it to them, as in His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And recite to them the news of Abraham﴾ (Q. 26:69). For they trace their lineage to him, peace be upon him, so perhaps by hearing his story they will desist from the vile deeds in which they are engaged.

﴿Indeed, he was a truthful one (siddiq)﴾ constantly adhering to truthfulness in everything he does and abstains from, or one who affirmed the truth very often, owing to the multitude of the unseen matters of God, the Exalted, that he affirmed as true, and His signs, His books, and His messengers. The sentence is a resumptive clause brought to give the reason for the requirement of the command, for describing him, peace be upon him, with this is among the motives for mentioning him.

﴿a prophet (nabiyyan)﴾ is another predicate of "kana" (was), qualifying and specifying the first, as is indicated by His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿of the prophets and the truthful ones﴾ (Q. 4:69)... the verse. That is: he was combining truthfulness (siddiqiyya) and prophethood (nubuwwa). Perhaps this ordering is for the sake of emphasis in guarding against the supposition that truthfulness is restricted to prophethood, since every prophet is a siddiq.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 42:**

﴿When he said﴾ is a *badal al-ishtimal* (a substitute noun that encompasses what it replaces, here "the substitution of inclusion") for ﴿Abraham﴾. What lies between them is an *i'tiraD* (a parenthetical insertion) that confirms what precedes it. Alternatively, it is connected to "kana" (was), or to "nabiyyan" (a prophet). The linking of remembrance to times, although the purpose is to remind of the events that occurred in them, has had its secret explained many times. That is: he was combining the two qualities (of truthfulness and prophethood) when he said ﴿to his father﴾, Azar, gently in the call and seeking to win him over.

﴿O my father﴾, i.e., O my father. The *ta'* (تاء) is a substitute for the *ya'* of possession (ياء الإضافة), and for this reason the two do not occur together. It has been said that one may say *ya abata* (يا أبتا) with an *alif*, because the *alif* is a substitute for the *ya'*.

﴿Why do you worship what does not hear﴾ your praise of it when you worship it, or your entreaty to it;

﴿and does not see﴾ your humility and submission before it. Or: it neither hears nor sees anything of what is heard or seen, so that what he mentioned is included by way of priority (دخولًا أوليًا).

﴿And does not avail you﴾ i.e., is not able to avail you,

﴿anything﴾ in bringing about benefit or warding off harm.

He, peace be upon him, followed in his call the best method and the most upright way, and argued against him with the most inventive argument, with good manners and beautiful character, so that he would not mount the back of obstinacy and stubbornness, nor turn away entirely from the path of right guidance. He asked him for the reason for his worship of something that the intellect of every sensible person, whether learned or ignorant, would consider foolish, and which refuses to incline toward it, let alone worship it, which is the furthest extreme of veneration, even though it is only fitting for one who possesses complete self-sufficiency and all-encompassing bounty: the Creator, the Provider, the Giver of life and death, the Rewarder and the Punisher. He drew attention to the fact that the sensible person must do everything he does for a sound motive and a sound purpose. If the thing were alive, discerning, hearing, seeing, able to benefit and harm, capable of conveying good and evil, even if it were possible for it to be so, the sound intellect would still disdain to worship it, even if it were the noblest of creatures, because it sees a being like itself in need and in submission to the overpowering, necessary power. So what is your opinion of a made lifeless object of stone or of wood, which has no attribute of living, nor any trace of it?

Then he invited him to follow him, so that he might guide him to the clear truth, since he (Azar) had not been granted a share of divine knowledge, nor was he independent in sound reasoning. (Abraham) began his call with the gentle persuasion and appeal for compassion that has already been mentioned, when he said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 43:

﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge what has not come to you﴾. He did not describe his father as utterly ignorant, even though he was in that state, nor describe himself as possessing surpassing knowledge, even though he did. Rather, he presented himself in the form of a companion of his, one more knowing of the conditions of the path they were both following. Thus he won him over gently, saying: ﴿so follow me, I will guide you to a path that is even (sawiyyan)﴾. That is, a straight path that leads to the most desirable goals and saves from the error that leads to the abysses of destruction and the places of ruin. Then he discouraged him from what he was upon by depicting it in a form that every rational person would reject, explaining that it is, while being utterly devoid of benefit, a drawing-in of great harm. For in reality it is the worship of Satan, since he is the one who commands it. So he said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 44:

﴿O my father, do not worship Satan﴾. For your worship of idols is worship of him (Satan), since it is he who adorns them for you and incites you to them. And His saying: ﴿Indeed, Satan has ever been to the Most Merciful a disobedient one﴾ is a justification for the requirement of the prohibition and a reinforcement of it, by declaring that he is rebellious against your Lord, who has bestowed upon you blessings of every kind. There is no doubt that whoever obeys a disobedient one is himself disobedient, and whoever is disobedient is deserving that the blessings be taken back from him and that he be punished. The use of the explicit noun in place of the pronoun is for the sake of increasing confirmation, and the restriction to mentioning his disobedience among all his transgressions is because it is the root of them, or because it is the result of his enmity toward Adam, peace be upon him, and his offspring. Thus his mention is a call to his father to beware of allying with him and obeying him, and the invoking of the title "the Most Merciful" serves to show the complete ugliness of his disobedience. And His saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 45:

﴿O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you﴾ — a warning about the evil outcome of what he was upon of worshipping Satan, namely that he would be afflicted with what his object of worship was afflicted with of the grievous punishment. The word "min" (from) is connected to a implied element that occurs as a qualifier of "punishment," emphasizing what the indefiniteness conveyed of inherent magnitude with additional magnitude (through its being attributed to the Merciful).
