The explicit mention of "al-Rahman" (the Most Merciful) is to indicate that the attribute of mercy does not prevent the descent of punishment, as in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿What has deceived you concerning your Lord, the Generous?﴾ ﴿So you would be to Satan a companion﴾, that is, a associate of his in the perpetual curse. The mention of fear is for courtesy, and to display concern for his matter.

﴿Qāla﴾ is a resumptive clause (istiʾnāf, a new sentence) built on a question arising from the beginning of the discourse, as if it were said: "What did his father say when he heard from him, peace be upon him, these advices that must be accepted?" So it was said: "He said," persisting in his obstinacy.

﴿"Are you turning away from my gods, Ibrahim?"﴾ That is: "Are you averse to them, and turning away from them?" The denial is directed at the very act of aversion, with a note of astonishment, as if turning away from them were something that no rational person would do, let alone encourage others to do. His saying ﴿"If you do not desist, I will surely stone you"﴾ is a threat and a warning against his admonition and reminder. That is: "By God, if you do not desist from what you were doing, namely forbidding the worship of them, I will surely stone you." It was also said: "with the tongue."

﴿"And leave me alone for a long time"﴾ That is: "Beware of me and leave me."

﴿Maliyyan﴾ means a long time, or "for a while, with the ability to go away."

﴿He said﴾ is a resumptive clause (istinaf, a new sentence that resumes the narrative), as has already been noted. ﴿Peace be upon you﴾ is a farewell and a disengagement, in the manner of repaying evil with good. That is, I will not harm you with anything hateful from now on, nor will I speak to you in a way that hurts you. But ﴿I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾, that is, I will petition Him to forgive you by granting you the success of repentance and guiding you to faith, as the reasoning in His words, ﴿And forgive my father﴾, followed by His words, ﴿Indeed he was among those who went astray﴾, hints at. Seeking forgiveness for an unbeliever in this sense, before it becomes clear that he will die in disbelief, is undoubtedly permissible. What is forbidden is to petition forgiveness for him while he remains in disbelief, for that has no justification by reason or by transmitted evidence. As for seeking forgiveness for him after his death in disbelief, reason does not reject it. What prevents it is the transmitted evidence (al-sam'), as in the report that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to his uncle Abu Talib: "I will not cease to ask forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden from it," whereupon there was revealed His words, ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ ... the verse.

There is a confusion about whether this promise came from Abraham (peace be upon him), and likewise his words, ﴿I will surely ask forgiveness for you﴾, and what followed from them, His words, ﴿And forgive my father﴾ ... the verse. It was before his hope in his father's faith was cut off, because the matter had not become clear to him, as in His words, ﴿So when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he disowned him﴾, as has passed in the commentary on Surat al-Tawba. His exception from the model to be followed in His words, ﴿except for the saying of Abraham to his father, "I will surely ask forgiveness for you"﴾, does not detract from the permissibility of this, but not because that was before the prohibition was revealed, or because of a promise he had made to him, as it has been said. For the prohibition was revealed only concerning seeking forgiveness after the matter has become clear, and Abraham's seeking forgiveness had been before it became clear, so the prohibition did not cover it at all. Nor does a promise of something forbidden remove its danger. Rather, what is meant by the model to be followed is what must be followed absolutely, because of the warning given against turning away from it in His words, ﴿There has certainly been for you a good example in them for whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day. And whoever turns away, indeed Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾. So his exception from that only indicates that it is not obligatory to petition faith for an unbeliever whose faith is hoped for, especially since that ended when the exception was stated, and no sensible person doubts this. As for the impermissibility of doing so before the matter became clear, the exception gives no clear indication of it. Directing the exception to the promise of seeking forgiveness, and not to the act of seeking forgiveness itself, is in His words, "And forgive my father" ... the verse, because it was that promise which had moved him, peace be upon him, to do so. The singling out of that promise for mention, rather than what occurred here, is because it came in the form of an emphatic oath. As for making the seeking of forgiveness revolve around it, and making disowning follow the clarity of the matter, its verification has already passed in the commentary on Surat al-Tawba.

His words, ﴿Indeed He has been gracious to me﴾, meaning: exceedingly kind in goodness. And ﴿al-Lutf﴾ (the Gracious, the Subtle) is a reason for what precedes it.

(p-269) ﴿And I will withdraw from you﴾, i.e., I will distance myself from you and from your people.

﴿And what you call upon besides Allah﴾, by migrating with my religion, since your admonitions have not affected you. ﴿And I will call upon my Lord﴾, i.e., I will worship Him alone. It is also permissible that it means His supplication mentioned in the commentary on Surah al-Shu'ara'. It is not far-fetched that it may also mean asking for a child, by His saying: ﴿My Lord, grant me from among the righteous﴾, as the preceding and the context support. ﴿It may be that I will not be, in calling upon my Lord, wretched﴾, i.e., frustrated, with my effort lost. In this there is an implicit allusion to their wretchedness in worshipping their gods. Beginning the statement with "it may be" (ʿasā) shows humility, observance of good manners, and an alerting to the reality of the truth: that answering and rewarding come by way of His bounty, Mighty and Majestic, not by way of obligation, and that the outcome is what counts. Such matters among the unseen things are specific to the All-Knowing, the All-Aware, and their subtlety is not hidden.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 49:

﴿So when he had withdrawn from them and from what they worshipped besides Allah﴾ by emigrating to al-Sham (Syria), ﴿We gave him Isaac and Jacob﴾ in place of those among his kinsmen, the disbelievers, whom he had left behind. However, not immediately after the emigration, for the well-known view is that the one granted to him at that time was Ishmael, peace be upon him, in accordance with the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So We gave him good news of a forbearing boy﴾, following his supplication in which he said: ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous﴾. The arrangement of the granting of these two upon his withdrawal here may serve to show the great magnitude of the blessings which Allah the Exalted bestowed upon him in exchange for those among his family and relatives from whom he withdrew, for these two are the two trees of the prophets, and they had children and grandchildren of great standing and of large number. This is so. It has also been narrated that when he, peace be upon him, set out for al-Sham, he first came to Harran, and he married Sarah, and she bore him Isaac, and Jacob was born to Isaac. The first is the closer and more evident.

﴿And each﴾, i.e., each one of the two of them or of them (all), and it is the first object of His saying: ﴿We made [each] a prophet﴾, which is placed before it for the purpose of specification, but not in relation to those other than them, rather in relation to some of them; i.e., each one of them We made a prophet, not some of them to the exclusion of others.

[Qur'an 19:50] "And We bestowed upon them of Our mercy," which is prophethood (nubuwwah). Its mention after the mention of their being made prophets indicates that it is among the forms of mercy. It has also been said that it is wealth and children, that is, the abundance of provision that was spread out for them. It has also been said that it is the Book. The more apparent view is that it is general, covering every good, religious and worldly, that they were given, of a kind that none among the worlds had been given.

"And We made for them a tongue of truthfulness, high (ʿaliyyan)," meaning that people take pride in them and praise them, in response to his supplication when he said: "And make for me a tongue of truthfulness among the later generations" [Qur'an 26:84]. By "tongue" is meant that by which speech is produced. "The tongue of the Arabs" is their language. Its attribution to truthfulness, and its description as elevated, serve to indicate that they deserve what people praise them for, and that their virtues remain undimmed despite the distance of eras, the changing of dynasties, and the transformation of creeds and sects.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 51:

﴿And mention in the Book Moses﴾ His mention is placed before the mention of Isma'il so that it would not be separated from the mention of Ya'qub, upon both of them be peace.

﴿Indeed, he was sincere (mukhlasan)﴾ a monotheist who made his worship sincere, free of association (shirk) and showing-off (riya'). Or, he submitted his face to God, the Exalted, and made himself sincere, free of anything other than Him. It has also been read as (mukhlasan), meaning that God, the Exalted, made him sincere (chose him purely).

﴿And he was a messenger (rasul), a prophet (nabi)﴾ God, the Exalted, sent him to the creation and he informed them about Him. For this reason He mentioned "messenger" before "prophet," even though it is more specific and higher in rank.

(p-270) ﴿And We called him from the right side of the Mount.﴾ Al-Tur: a mountain between Egypt and Madyan. "Al-Ayman" is an adjective of "al-janib" (the side), meaning: We called him from its right-hand side, which is the one adjoining the right of Musa (peace be upon him); or from its blessed side, from the blessing (al-yumn). The meaning of His calling him from it is that speech was addressed to him from that direction.

﴿And We brought him near as a confidant.﴾ It is a drawing-near of honour: his state (peace be upon him) is likened to the state of one whom a king brings near for private conversation and chooses for close companionship. "Najiyyan," meaning one who converses privately, is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to one of the two pronouns in "nadaynahu" or "qarrabnahu." It was also said: "elevated," because it is narrated that he (peace be upon him) was raised above the heavens until he heard the scratching of the pen.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 53:

﴿And We gave him, out of Our mercy,﴾ i.e., on account of Our mercy and Our compassion toward him, or some part of Our mercy.

﴿his brother﴾ i.e., (giving him) support and backing from his brother, in response to his supplication when he said: ﴿And appoint for me a minister from my family, ﴾ ﴿Aaron, my brother﴾, not himself, because he (Aaron) was older than him, peace be upon them both. On the first reading, "his brother" is the object of "wahabna" (We gave), and on the second reading it is an apposition (badal) to the words of His Exalted saying ﴿Aaron﴾, which is an explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayan) to it. And His Exalted saying ﴿a prophet﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 54:

﴿And mention in the Book Ismail﴾. His mention is separated from the mention of his father and his brother in order to display the complete care given to his matter, by presenting him independently. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he was true to his promise﴾ is a justification for the requirement of the command. And the presentation of him, upon him be peace, with this attribute is due to the complete fame he had for it; and it is enough that he promised patience in the face of the slaughter by saying: ﴿You will find me, God willing, among the patient﴾, and he fulfilled it. ﴿And he was a messenger, a prophet﴾. In this there is an indication that a messenger does not have to be a bringer of a sharia (shari'ah, sacred law), for the sons of Ibrahim, upon him be peace, were upon his sharia.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 55:

﴿And he used to enjoin on his family prayer and zakat﴾, giving precedence to what is more important. That is, a man should first devote himself to perfecting his own soul, and then to those closest to him. Thus Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And warn your nearest kinsmen﴾, and [He says]: "Enjoin your family to prayer", and ﴿Save yourselves and your families from a Fire﴾. The intention is to perfect everyone by perfecting them, since they are an example to be followed. It has also been said: his family here means his ummah, for the prophets, peace be upon them, are the fathers of their nations. ﴿And he was with his Lord well-pleasing﴾, because of his possessing the sublime attributes, of which the praiseworthy qualities mentioned are part.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 56:

﴿And mention in the Book Idris﴾. He is the descendant (sibt) of Shith (Seth) and the grandfather of the father of Nuh (Noah), for Nuh is the son of Lamak, son of Matushalh, son of Akhnukh. He is Idris, peace be upon him. His derivation from "al-dars" (study, recitation) is rejected by the prohibition of his declension (man' sarfih). Yet it is not far-fetched that his meaning in that language was close to that, and so he was given this title because of his abundant study. It is related that Allah the Exalted sent down to him thirty scrolls (sahifah), and that he was the first to write with the pen, and that he looked into the science of the stars and calculation.

﴿Indeed, he was a truthful one (siddiqan)﴾, constant in truthfulness in all his states.

﴿A prophet (nabiyyan)﴾: this is another predicate (khabar) of "kana", specifying the first, since not every truthful person is a prophet.

(p-271) ﴿And We raised him to a lofty station﴾. This is the honour of prophethood and nearness to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. It was also said: it is the elevation of rank through a good mention in this world, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We raised high your remembrance﴾. It was also said: it is Paradise, and it was said: it is the sixth heaven or the fourth. It is narrated from Ka'b and others concerning the reason for the raising of Idris, peace be upon him, that he was once asked about a matter, and the heat of the sun struck him, so he said: "O Lord, I walked in it for one day, and what befell me from it has befallen me; how then will one who carries it for a journey of five hundred years in a single day fare?! O Allah, lighten his burden and its heat for him." So when the angel (al-malik) awoke, he found from the lightness of the sun and its heat what he did not recognize. He said: "O Lord, what did You decree concerning it?" He said: "My servant Idris asked Me to lighten its burden and its heat for you, and I granted him that." He said: "O Lord, make between me and him a close friendship (khullah)." So Allah, exalted is He, permitted him, and He raised him to the heavens.

﴿Ulā'ika﴾ (أُولَئِكَ, "those") is a demonstrative referring to those mentioned in the noble surah. The sense of distance in the demonstrative indicates their elevated rank and the remoteness of their station in excellence. It is the subject (mubtada'). The words ﴿alladhīna an'ama Allāhu 'alayhim﴾ ("those upon whom Allah has bestowed favor") are its qualifying clause (ṣifah), meaning that Allah bestowed upon them every kind of favor, religious and worldly, as has been alluded to in summary. The words ﴿min al-nabiyyīn﴾ ("of the prophets") are an explanatory clarification (bayān) of the relative pronoun. The words ﴿min dhurriyyati Ādam﴾ ("of the offspring of Adam") are a substitute (badal) for it, with the preposition repeated. It is also permissible for the "min" here to be partitive (tab'īd), because those upon whom favor was bestowed are more general than the prophets and more specific than the offspring.

﴿Wa-mimman ḥamalnā ma'a Nūḥ﴾ ("and of those whom We carried with Noah"): that is, and of the offspring of those whom We carried with him specifically, who are all except Idrīs (ʿalayhi al-salām), for Ibrāhīm was of the offspring of Sām ibn Nūḥ.

﴿Wa-min dhurriyyati Ibrāhīm﴾ ("and of the offspring of Abraham"): they are the rest.

﴿Wa-Isrā'īl﴾ ("and Israel") is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon Ibrāhīm, meaning and of the offspring of Israel. Among them were Mūsā, Hārūn, Zakariyyā, Yaḥyā and ʿĪsā (ʿalayhim al-salām). In this there is evidence that the children of daughters are counted among the offspring.

﴿Wa-mimman hadaynā wa-ajtabaynā﴾ ("and of those whom We guided and chose"): that is, and of those among the number whom We guided to the truth and chose for prophethood and honor. The words ﴿idhā tutlā 'alayhim āyātu al-Raḥmān kharrū sujjadan wa-bukiyyā﴾ ("when the verses of the Most Merciful are recited to them, they fall down prostrating and weeping") are the predicate (khabar) of ﴿Ulā'ika﴾. It is also permissible for the predicate to be the relative clause, and this would be a resumptive statement (isti'nāf) given to explain their fear of Allah and their humility before Him, together with their state of high rank, lofty station, nobility of lineage, perfection of soul, and nearness to Allah, Mighty is His authority. ﴿Sujjadan wa-bukiyyā﴾ ("prostrating and weeping") are two circumstantial states (ḥāl) of the pronoun in ﴿kharrū﴾, meaning prostrating and weeping. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Recite the Qur'an and weep; and if you do not weep, then feign weeping." The word bukiyy is the plural of bākin, as sujjad is the plural of sājid. Its original form was bukuwy; the waw and the yā' came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukūn, so the waw was changed into yā', the yā' was assimilated into the yā' (idghām), and the kāf was given a kasra to match the yā'.

It was read as ﴿yutlā﴾ (يُتْلى) with a yā' prefix, because the feminine gender here is not real (ghayr ḥaqīqī). It was also read as ﴿bikiyyā﴾ (بِكِيًّا) with a kasra on the bā' for harmony (ittibā'). The scholars said: the one prostrating should, in his prostration, supplicate with what suits its verse. So here he says: "O Allah, make me among Your servants upon whom You have bestowed favor, who are guided, who prostrate to You, and who weep when Your verses are recited." In the verse of al-Isrā' he says: "O Allah, make me among those who weep toward You and are humble before You." In the prostration verse of Tanzīl (al-Sajdah) he says: "O Allah, make me among those who prostrate to Your face and glorify You with Your praise, and I seek refuge in You from being among those who are arrogant toward Your command."

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 59:**

(p-272) ﴿Then there succeeded them a succession (khalf)﴾. It is said that for a good offspring one uses *khalaf* with a fatha on the lam, and for an evil offspring *khalf* with a sukun, meaning: he succeeded them, and there came after them an evil progeny.

﴿They neglected the prayer﴾. It is also read as (الصَّلَواتِ) *al-salawat* (plural), meaning: they abandoned it, or they delayed it beyond its time.

﴿And followed their desires﴾, such as drinking wine, permitting marriage to a sister from the father's side, and immersion in various kinds of sins. And from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him: they built the plastered (*mashid*) buildings, rode the admired (*manzur*) mounts, and wore the famous (*mashhur*) garments.

﴿So they will meet with ghayy﴾, that is, evil. For among the Arabs every evil is *ghayy*, and every good is *rashad* (right guidance), as in his saying:

*Whoever meets with good, people will praise his affair,*
*and whoever goes astray (yaghwa) will not lack a blamer for his error.*

And from al-Dahhak: the recompense of *ghayy*, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿will meet with sin (athaman)﴾, that is, the recompense of sin; or *ghayy* as a departure from the path of Paradise. It is also said: *Ghayy* is a valley in Hell from which its other valleys seek refuge. And His saying, Exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 60:

﴿Except for one who repents, believes, and does righteous deeds﴾ indicates that the verse concerns the disbelievers. ﴿Those﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) in terms of its being characterized by what is within the scope of the relative clause (al-silah), and with the sense of distance that it carries, as has been mentioned many times before. That is: ﴿those﴾ who are described as possessing repentance, faith, and righteous deeds.

﴿will enter the Garden﴾ by the necessary consequence of the binding promise. It is also read (yudkhalun), in the passive voice (al-bina' lil-maf'ul).

﴿and they will not be wronged in the least﴾ meaning: they will not be deprived of any part of the reward for their deeds; or, they will not be diminished in the least from the diminution [of their reward]. In this there is an indication that their previous disbelief does not harm them nor diminish their rewards.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 61:

﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "al-Jannah" (the Garden), a substitution of part for whole (badal al-ba'd), because the gardens include it. What lies between them is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraad). Alternatively, it is in the accusative on the basis of praise (nasb 'ala al-madh). It has also been read in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e., "they are," or "those are gardens" ... etc. Or it is a subject whose predicate is "which the Most Merciful promised to His servants" ... etc. It has also been read as "Jannata 'Adnin" in the accusative and nominative, and "'Adn" is a proper name for the meaning of 'adn, which is residence (al-iqamah). Just as "Fayna," "Sahar," and "Amsi" are proper names for the meanings of fayna (a moment), which is the present hour you are in, sahar (the pre-dawn), and amsi (yesterday), for those who do not declare them diptotic (ghayr al-munsarif), so it takes the same course as 'adn. Or it is the proper name of the land, the Garden specifically. Were it not so, the substitution of what is annexed to it, "al-Jannah," without a description would not be permissible according to others than the Basrians, nor would describing it with the words of the Exalted, ﴿which the Most Merciful promised to His servants﴾, and making it a substitute for it, would be contrary to what is apparent, for the relative clause (al-mawsul) has the status of a derived noun (mushtaqq), and they have explicitly stated that substitution with a derived noun is weak. The mention of the title "the Mercy" is to indicate that its promise and its fulfilment stem from the complete vastness of His mercy, the Exalted.

The "ba'" in the words of the Exalted, ﴿bil-ghayb﴾ (in the unseen), is connected to a hidden element that is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun referring to the Gardens, or from His servants, i.e., He promised them to them while it was (or they were) in a state of being unseen by them, not present, or they were absent from it and did not see it; they believed in it merely by being informed. Or it is connected to a hidden element which is the cause of the promise, i.e., He promised them it because of their faith.

﴿Indeed, His promise was﴾, i.e., what was promised by Him, whatever it was, so the promised Gardens enter into it as a primary entry. Since they are a place to which one returns, it was said: ﴿coming (ma'tiyyan)﴾, i.e., those promised to it will inevitably come to it without failure. It was also said that it is an object in the sense of a subject, and it was said: ma'tiyyan, i.e., a completed fulfilled thing, from "one who came to him with kindness," i.e., did it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 62:

﴿They shall not hear therein any vain talk﴾, i.e., superfluous speech without any benefit in it. It is a metaphor (kinayah) for the fact that vain talk does not proceed from its people, and it contains an admonition that vain talk is something that one should, as far as possible, avoid in this abode.

﴿Except the word "Salam" (peace)﴾ is an exceptive clause of disconnection (istithna' munqati'), i.e., but they hear the greeting of the angels to them, or the greeting of some of them to others. Or it is a connected exception by way of conditioning on the impossible, i.e., they do not hear any vain talk; but since it is impossible for "salam" to be vain talk, their hearing of it is impossible altogether, as in the saying of the poet:

"There is no fault in them, except that their swords are, because of them, notched from the clashing of the battalions."

Or it is taken that its meaning is the supplication for safety, and they are free of it, in terms of vain talk apparently; its benefit is only honouring them. The words of the Most High: ﴿And for them their provision is therein morning and evening﴾ come in the customary manner of the affluent in this abode. It has also been said that what is meant is the continuity and abundance of their provision, since there is in it neither morning nor evening.

This is the commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 63:

﴿Such is the Garden﴾ is a subject and predicate, brought in to magnify the status of the Garden and to specify its people. For the notion of distance contained in the demonstrative indicates the remoteness of its station and the loftiness of its rank.

﴿which We cause to inherit﴾ i.e., We cause to inherit it.

﴿those of Our servants who were God-fearing (taqiyy)﴾ i.e., We preserve it for them on account of their God-consciousness and let them enjoy it, just as we preserve for the heir the property of the one who bequeathed it and let him enjoy it. Inheritance (al-wirathah) is the strongest of the terms used for possession and entitlement, in that it is not followed by revocation, reclaiming, or annulment. It has also been said: the God-conscious inherit from the Garden the dwellings that were intended for the people of the Fire had they believed and obeyed, as an increase in their honour. And it has been read as nuwarrithu (with the doubled letter), with emphasis.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 64:

﴿And we do not descend except by the command of your Lord.﴾ This is a narration of the words of Jibril (Gabriel) when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was slow to receive revelation, after he was asked about the People of the Cave, Dhul-Qarnayn, and the Spirit. He did not know how to answer, and he hoped that revelation would come to him concerning them, so it was delayed from him for forty days, or fifteen, and that caused him severe hardship. The polytheists said: "His Lord has abandoned him and turned away from him." Then the explanation came down, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent down this verse and Surat al-Duha. Al-tanzil (the descending) means descending gradually (ʿalā mahl), because it is the intransitive form (mutawaʿ) of al-tanzil (causing to descend). It may also be applied to descending in general, just as tanzil is applied to inzal (sending down). The meaning is: "We do not descend at one time after another except by the command of Allah Most High, according to what His wisdom requires." It was also read as (وَما يَتَنَزَّلُ) with the ya', the pronoun referring to the revelation.

﴿To Him belongs what is before us, what is behind us, and what is between that﴾: this is what we are in of places and times. We do not move from one place to another, nor descend in one time rather than another, except by His command and will.

﴿And your Lord is never forgetful﴾: i.e., never abandoning you. The meaning is that the non-descent was only because of the absence of a command to do so, for a far-reaching wisdom in it, and not because of His abandoning you and bidding you farewell, as the disbelievers claimed. In repeating the name of the Lord, which indicates the conveying to its fitting perfection, attributed to the pronoun of him (peace be upon him), there is honour for him and an indication of the reason for the ruling, which is not hidden. It has also been said: the beginning of the verse is a narration of the words of the righteous when they enter Paradise, addressing one another in a manner of exultation and joy. The meaning: "We do not enter Paradise except by the command and grace of Allah Most High, and He is the Owner of all affairs, past, future and present. What we have found and what we find of His grace and bounty." His saying, Most High, "And your Lord is never forgetful" is an affirmation of their words from Allah Most High's side, i.e., He was never forgetful of the deeds of those who worked, nor of the reward He promised them for them. His saying, Most High:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 65:

﴿The Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them.﴾ This is an explanation of the impossibility of forgetfulness on the part of Allah, exalted is He. For He in whose hand is the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, how could it be imagined that heedlessness and forgetfulness should hover around the sanctuary of His glory (subuhat)? It is either the predicate of an omitted subject, or an apposition (badal) to "your Lord." The "fa" (then) in His words, exalted is He: ﴿So worship Him and be steadfast in His worship﴾, indicates that what follows it is the consequence of the two commands, arising from what precedes it, namely His being the Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them. It has also been said: arising from His being one who does not abandon him, peace be upon him, or one who does not forget the deeds of those who act. The meaning is: when you have come to know Him, exalted is He, by what has been mentioned of perfect lordship, then worship Him, and so on. For the obligation of knowing Him thus, as the basis for worshipping Him, is beyond doubt. Or: when you know that He, exalted is He, does not forget you, or forget the deeds of those who act, whoever they may be, then turn to His worship and be steadfast in its hardships, and do not grieve over the delay of revelation or the mockery of the disbelievers, for He watches over you, cares for you, and is gentle with you in this world and the Hereafter. The transitive use of "isbar" (be steadfast) with the preposition "li-" rather than the preposition of elevation (ʿala), as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿and be steadfast in it﴾, is because it implies the sense of firmness in worship in the face of the calamities and hardships that confront it, like your saying to one who fights a duel: "isbir li-qarnika" (stand firm against your opponent), that is: hold your ground against him in the face of his hardships directed at you.

﴿Do you know of anyone who is named like Him?﴾ The "sami" (namesake) is the one who shares the name. The apparent meaning here is that it refers to one who shares a particular name by which He, exalted is He, has designated Himself, namely "the Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them." The intent of denying and negating knowledge is the denial and negation of what is known, in the most emphatic and forceful manner. The sentence thus confirms what the "fa" implies, namely the causal basis of His general lordship for the obligation of worshipping Him, indeed for the obligation of restricting worship to Him, exalted is He, by clarifying His sole possession of that name, and the total negation of its application to another, whether truly or falsely. It has also been said: the intent is one who shares the noble name (al-Jalil, i.e. Allah), for the polytheists, despite their extreme obstinacy, never named the idol with the divine name at all. And it has been said: it is one who shares the name "God" (ilah), and the intent of "naming" is naming in truth. The meaning then is: do you know anything that is named as deserving divinity? As for naming in falsehood, it is as if no naming were made. Thus the sentence confirms the obligation of worship on account of what the two noble names imply of the entitlement to worship, so reflect.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 66:

﴿And man says⦆ Here "man" (al-insan) may mean either the entire human species, and the attribution of the saying to all of them is because the saying exists among them, even if not all of them said it, as one says: "The Banu so-and-so killed so-and-so," when the killer was only one of them. Or it may mean a specific portion of them that is known, namely the disbelievers, or Ubayy ibn Khalaf, for he took decayed bones and crumbled them and said: "Muhammad claims that we will be resurrected after we die and return to this state." That is, he says, by way of denial and disbelief: ﴿Is it that when I have died, I will indeed be brought forth alive?⦆ That is, I will be raised from the earth, or from the state of death. The placing of the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) before the interrogative particle of denial (harf al-inkar) is because what is denied is the occurrence of what comes after death at the time of life. Its being in the accusative case (intisabuhu) is governed by a verb indicated by "ukhrij" (I will be brought forth), not by "ukhrij" itself, because what follows the lam (the lam of emphasis) does not operate on what precedes it. Here the lam is purely for emphasis (li-l-tawkid), stripped of the meaning of the present tense, just as the hamza and lam are free of meaning for compensation in "ya Allah." Thus its conjunction with the particle of the future (harf al-istiqbal) is permissible. It has also been read: "idha ma mittu" with a single hamza, kasra-marked, as a statement (ʿala al-khabar).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 67:

﴿Does not man remember﴾ from the remembrance (dhikr) that is meant as reflection (tafakkur). The use of the explicit noun in the place of the pronoun serves to increase the affirmation and to indicate that humanity is itself a motive for reflecting upon what has befallen him of the matters of creation, which turn him away, by being uprooted, from the aforementioned statement. This is the secret of attributing it to the genus, or to the individual under that title. The hamza is for rebuking denial, and the waw (p-275) is for conjoining the negated clause to an implied antecedent indicated by "says": i.e., does he say that, and not remember?

﴿That We created him before﴾ i.e., before the state in which he is now, which is the state of his existence.

﴿and he was nothing﴾ i.e., while the reality is that he was not anything at all at that time. Since We created him while he was in that state, which is wholly contrary to creation, and since it is farther from occurring, then to resurrect him by gathering the scattered materials and bringing into being the like of the accidents that were in them is more fitting and more evident. So why does he not remember, and thereby fall into what he falls into of denial? It is read "yudhakkaru" and "yatadhakkaru", in accordance with the original form.

﴿So by your Lord﴾: His swearing by His own name, exalted are His names, with the name placed in apposition to the pronoun referring to him, peace be upon him, serves to confirm the matter by indicating its cause, to magnify his station, ﷺ, and to elevate his rank.

﴿We will surely gather them﴾: That is, We will surely assemble those who are to be driven to the place of gathering (al-mahshar) after We have brought them forth from the earth alive. In this there is an affirmation of resurrection by a demonstrative (burhani) method, in the most eloquent and emphatic form, as though it were a clear matter that needs no explicit statement. What requires explanation is what follows it of terrors.

﴿And the devils﴾: This is coordinated with the pronoun in the accusative (al-damir al-mansub), or it is an object of accompaniment (maf'ul ma'ah). It is related that the disbelievers will be gathered together with their companions among the devils who used to lead them astray, each one with his devil in a chain. Although this is specific to them, it is permissible to attribute it to the whole category, on the basis that when they are gathered, and the disbelievers among them are joined with the devils, they have all been gathered together. Likewise, it is permissible to attribute a reported statement to a group when only some of its members spoke it.

﴿Then We will surely bring them forth around Hell on their knees﴾: So that the blessed may see what Allah, exalted is He, has saved them from, and thus increase in joy and delight, and so that the wretched may receive what they have stored up as provision for their return, and increase in rage at the blessed returning away from them to the abode of reward, and at their gloating over them. Al-jithiyy is the plural of jathin, from jatha, meaning he sat upon his knees. Its original form is "jithuww" with two waws. Their combination after two dammas was felt to be heavy, so the thaʾ was given a kasra for lightness; the first waw was then changed into a ya' because it was sukun and preceded by a kasra. A waw and a ya' then came together, one of them preceded by sukun, so the waw was changed into a ya', the first ya' was assimilated into it, and the jim was given a kasra to match what follows it (ittiba'). It has also been read with a damma on the jim. Its accusative form is a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun that is expressed, meaning: We will surely bring them forth around Hell, kneeling on their knees, because of the terror of the moment of confrontation that will overwhelm them. Or because it belongs to the things that accompany being made to stand for reckoning before arriving at reward and punishment, for the people of the standing-place are on their knees, as indicated by the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And you will see every nation kneeling﴾, as is customary in places of mutual pleading. If the word "man" (al-insan) is taken to mean the disbelievers, then perhaps they will be driven from the standing-place to the edge of Hell on their knees, as a humiliation to them, or because of their inability to stand due to the severity that has befallen them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 69:

﴿Then We will surely drag out from every sect﴾ i.e., from every community that adhered to a religion among the religions.

﴿Which of them is most rebellious against the Most Merciful?﴾ i.e., whoever among them is most disobedient and most insolent. So We cast them into it (the Fire). The mention of "the most" (ashadd) is an indication that He, exalted is He, pardons some of the people of disobedience. And on the basis of interpreting "al-insan" (the human being) as the disbelievers, the meaning is: We distinguish from every group among them the most disobedient of them, then the most insolent of them, and We cast them into the Fire in order of rank; or We cause each of them to enter its appropriate tier.

"Ayyuhum" (which of them) is indeclinable (mabni) on the dammah according to Sibawayh, because its original status is to be indeclinable like the rest of the relative-type words (al-mawsulat); but it has been treated as declinable (u'rib) by analogy with "kull" (each) and "ba'd" (some), due to the obligation of its being in a construct phrase (idafah). When its initial element (sadr silatihi) is omitted, its deficiency increases, so it returns to its original status. Its position is accusative (mansub al-mahall) by "lananza'anna" (We will surely drag out), and for this reason it has been read in the accusative. According to others, it is in the nominative (marfu') as a subject (mubtada'), with the interrogative sense, and its predicate is "ashaddu" (most), and the clause is reported speech (mahkiyyah). The estimated meaning is: "We will surely drag out from every sect those who will be asked, 'Which of them is most rebellious?'" Or it is suspended from action (mu'allaq 'anha), with "lananza'anna" governing it, since it contains the meaning of distinction (tamyiz) which is necessary for knowledge. Or it is a resumptive new clause (musta'nafah).

The verb governs "every sect" through the added "min" (from), or in the sense of "We will surely drag out some of every sect," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and We gave them of Our mercy﴾. The "'ala" (against) is for explanation (bayan), so it is connected to an omitted element, as if a questioner had asked: "Against whom did they transgress?" and it was answered: "Against the Most Merciful." Or it is connected to "a'fal" (more), and likewise the "ba'" in His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 70:

﴿Then We are most knowing of those who are most deserving of being burned therein.﴾ That is: they are most deserving of its burning (ṣilliyihā), or their burning (ṣilliyyuhum) is most deserving of the Fire. They are those who are pulled out (al-muntaza'ūn). It is also permissible that by them, and by those who are the most insolent of them in rebellion (ʿitiyyan), are meant the leaders of the sects (ru'asa' al-shiya'), for their punishment is doubled because of their own misguidance and their misguiding of others. Ṣiliyy is like ʿitiyy in form and in its irregular (iʿlal) treatment. It has also been read with a ḍamma on the ṣad (ṣulliyy).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 71:

﴿And there is none of you﴾ This is a shift (iltifat) in address, to show increased attention to the content of the statement. It has also been said that it is an address to people in general, without any shift toward what was previously mentioned. The first view is supported by the fact that it has been recited as (وَإنْ مِنهُمْ, "and there is none of them"), meaning: there is none of you, O human being.

﴿except that he will approach it﴾ That is, he will reach it and be present close to it, passing by it. The believers will pass by it while it is extinguished (khamidah), and it will be cool (wa-tahurru) for others. It is narrated from Jabir that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about it and said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, some of them will say to others: Did not our Lord promise us that we would approach the Fire? It will be said to them: You have approached it, and it is extinguished."

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿Those are kept far from it﴾, what is meant is that they are kept distant from its punishment. It has also been said: their approaching it means passing over the bridge (sirat) stretched over it.

﴿It was﴾ That is, their approaching it.

﴿a decree decided by your Lord﴾ That is, a matter that is binding (mahtum), which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, made obligatory upon Himself, and decreed that it must definitely take place. It has also been said: He swore an oath concerning it.

Then We shall deliver those who were conscious of God (ittaqaw), [meaning those who avoided] disbelief and sins, from the state in which they were, kneeling on their knees, in the manner mentioned earlier. Then they will be led to Paradise. It is also read as (nunajji) with the lightened form, and as (yunjī) and (yunjā) in the passive voice. It is also read as (thammata) with a fatha on the thāʾ, meaning: there, We shall deliver them.

﴿And We shall leave the wrongdoers﴾ in disbelief and sins ﴿therein, kneeling﴾, cast down upon their faces, just as they were. It has been said: in this there is evidence that what is meant by "coming to it" (al-wurūd) is kneeling around it, and that the believers will separate from the wicked after they have knelt around it, while the wicked will be thrown into it in their [kneeling] postures. And His Exalted saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 73:

﴿And when Our clear verses are recited to them...﴾ ...to the end of the verse. This is a narration of what they said upon hearing the verses that expose to them the horror of their state and the grimness of their end; that is: "And when they are recited to the polytheists."

﴿Our verses﴾, among which are those verses that speak of the good state of the believers and the bad state of the disbelievers. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿clear﴾ means: well-arranged in wording, clear in meanings by themselves, or by the clarification of the Messenger (ﷺ), or clear in their inimitability. It is a emphasizing circumstantial (ḥāl) clause relating to "Our verses."

﴿Those who disbelieved said﴾, that is: they said. The placing of the relative noun in the position of the pronoun is to draw attention to the fact that they said what they said while disbelieving in what was recited to them and rejecting it. Or it means: those among them who were persistent in disbelief and habituated to arrogance and obstinacy, namely al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and his followers, the wicked (al-fajarah). The "lam" in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿to those who believed﴾ is for communication (lam al-tabligh), as in similar usage such as His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And their prophet said to them﴾. It has also been said that it is the lam of purpose (lam al-ajal), as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed: "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it"﴾; that is: they said it for their sake and concerning them. The first is preferable, because their saying is not only concerning the believers, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Which of the two groups﴾, that is: the believers and the disbelievers, as if they said: "Which of us is ﴿better in position﴾, we or you?", that is: in place. It has been read with a dammah on the mim, meaning: a place of residence and abode.

﴿And better in assembly﴾, that is: in gathering and company. It is narrated that they used to comb their hair, anoint it, perfume themselves, and adorn themselves with fine adornments, then they would say this to the poor believers, intending by it that their superiority in state and their better attainment is something that cannot be denied, and that this is due to their honour with God, glory be to Him, and their nearness to Him, since it is the measure of superiority, inferiority, elevation and lowliness. And that it necessarily entails the humiliation of the believers before Him, exalted is He, because of the deficiency of their immediate portion. This barren analogy and corrupt opinion is only because they are ignorant people who know only the outward appearance of the worldly life, and that is the extent of their knowledge. So this was refuted against them from His side, exalted is He, by His saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 74:

﴿How many generations We have destroyed before them, who were better in furnishings and in appearance.﴾ That is: many of the generations who were superior to them in what they boasted of of worldly fortunes, such as ʿAd, Thamud and their likes among the insolent nations. Before these, We destroyed them with various kinds of punishment. Had what We gave them been due to their honour with Us, We would not have done to them what We did. In this there is a threat and warning that is not hidden; it is as if it were said: let these also wait for the like of that. Thus "kam" (how many) is the object of "ahlakna" (We destroyed), and "min qarn" (from a generation) is an explanation of its vagueness. The people of every age are a "qarn" (generation) for those who come after them, because they precede them; it is derived from "qarn al-dabbah" (the horn of the animal), which is its front part. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿who were better in furnishings﴾, is in the place of accusative as an attribute of "kam". "Athathan" (furnishings) is a specification of the relation, and it means the household goods. It has been said: it is what is new of them, while "al-khurthi" is what has been worn out and become decayed. "Al-riʾy" (appearance) is the sight, a form derived from "al-ruʾyah" (seeing), like "al-tihn" for what is ground. It was read as "riyyan" by converting the hamza into a yaʾ and assimilating it, or it is from "al-riyy", which is blessing and affluence. It was also read as "riyʾan" by conversion, and "riya" by dropping the hamza, and "ziyyan" with the dotted zay, from "al-ziyy", which means gathering, for it is an expression for the gathered beauties.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 75:

﴿Say: Whoever is in error, let the Most Merciful extend for him an extension.﴾ When He had explained the outcome of the affair of the destroyed nations, together with what they had of enjoyment of the various kinds of immediate pleasures, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to answer these boasters, who took pride in what they possessed of such pleasures, by explaining the final outcome of the affair of both groups. This is either in a general manner, encompassing them and others who are immersed in and delighted by fleeting worldly pleasure, with "whoever" being understood in its generality; or in a specific manner directed at them, with "whoever" being an expression for them, and describing them with being firmly established (in error) serves to censure them and to indicate the cause of the ruling. That is: whoever is firmly established in error, submerged in ignorance and heedlessness of the consequences of affairs, then let the Most Merciful extend for him, that is, He extends for him and gives him respite with long life, the granting of wealth, and empowerment in dealings. The expression is put in the form of a command to signify that this is something that ought to be done in accordance with the requirement of wisdom, to cut off excuses, as indicated by the saying of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿Did We not give you a life long enough for whoever would take heed to take heed?﴾ Or it is for istidraj (gradual leading on), as is spoken of by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin.﴾ It has also been said that what is meant is the supplication for extension and prolongation. And taking "being firmly established in error" into account, because extension is not given except to those who persist in it, for many a one who is astray is guided by Allah, the Exalted and Majestic. The mention of the title "the Most Merciful" is because extension is among the rulings of worldly mercy. The saying of the Exalted: ﴿until, when they see what they are promised﴾ is a limit (ghayah) for the extended extension itself, not for the saying of the boasters, as has been said, since there is in it no extension by its essence, which is evident, nor continuity by way of repetition, since it falls within the scope of the answer of "idha" (when). The plurality of the pronoun in the two verbs is in consideration of the meaning of "man" (whoever), just as the singularity in the first two pronouns is in consideration of its wording. The saying of the Exalted: ﴿either the punishment or the Hour﴾ is a detailing of what is promised, a substitution from it by way of badal (substitution). For it is either the worldly punishment, by the victory of the Muslims over them, their domination of them, and their punishing them by killing and taking captive; or it is the Day of Resurrection and what they will receive therein of disgrace and retribution, in the manner of preventing vacancy without preventing combination, for the otherworldly punishment never separates from them in any state. The saying of the Exalted: ﴿then they will know﴾ is the answer to the condition. The clause is reported after "until", that is: until, when they witness what they are promised of the worldly punishment, or the otherworldly alone, then they will know at that time ﴿who is worse in position﴾ of the two groups, by their witnessing the matter contrary to what they were estimating, so they will know that they are worse in position and not better in station.

﴿And weaker in force﴾, that is, in group and helpers, not better in assembly as they were claiming. It is not meant that they have there weak soldiers; no. ﴿And they had no company to help them apart from Allah, nor were they able to defend themselves.﴾ This was mentioned only as a refutation of what they used to claim, that they had helpers among the notables and supporters among the good, and they would boast of that in gatherings and assemblies.

The statement "And Allah increases in guidance those who are guided" is a resumptive clause (*kalam mustanaf*), brought in to explain the state of those who are guided, after explaining the state of those who go astray. It has also been said that it is coordinated (*'atf*) with "let him extend," because that phrase carries the sense of a report, as you have come to know. It is as if it were said: whoever is in error, Allah extends for him, and He increases those who are guided in guidance. This is like His saying: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾.

It has also been said that it is coordinated with the conditional clause reported after "said." It is as if, when He explained that the respite and enjoyment of life given to the disbeliever is not due to his merit, He followed this with an explanation that the deficiency in the believer's share of these things is not due to his deficiency, but because Allah intended for him what is better than that. His saying: ﴿And the enduring good deeds are better﴾ is, under both the resumptive and the coordinated readings, a resumptive clause coming from Allah, the Exalted, to explain the excellence of the deeds of those who are guided. It is not included within the scope of the speech that was dictated (to the Prophet), because of His saying: ﴿with your Lord﴾. That is, the acts of obedience whose benefits remain and whose rewards endure. Among them, it has been said, are the five daily prayers, and it has been said that the words "Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, and Allah is greatest" are better with Allah, the Exalted.

The mention of the title of Lordship together with its being attached to his pronoun (ﷺ) is to honour him (ﷺ). ﴿As a reward﴾: that is, a return, compared with what the disbelievers enjoy of blessings that are deficient and perishing, in which they take pride, especially since its outcome is lasting bliss, while the outcome of theirs is perpetual regret and painful punishment. As indicated by His saying: ﴿and better in outcome﴾: that is, a place of return and well-being. The repetition of "better" is for greater emphasis on explaining the excellence and as an affirmation of it. In the use of the comparative, although what belongs to the disbelievers has no excellence at all in its outcome, there is a mockery of them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 77:

﴿Have you seen the one who disbelieved in Our signs?﴾ That is: in Our signs, of which the signs of resurrection are part. It was revealed concerning al-'As ibn Wa'il. Khabbab ibn al-Aratt had a debt owed to him by him, so he demanded it, and he said: "Not until you disbelieve in Muhammad (ﷺ)." He said: "No, by God, I will not disbelieve in him, alive or dead, nor when I am raised up." He said: "When you are raised up, come to me, and then I will have wealth and children there, and I will give you." In another narration he said: "I will not disbelieve in him until He causes you to die and then you are raised up." He said: "Indeed I am dying, and then raised." He said: "Yes." He said: "Leave me until I die and am raised, and then I will be given wealth and children, and I will pay you," and so it was revealed. The interrogative particle (alif-hamza) here is for expressing wonder at his condition and signalling that it is of such strangeness and monstrousness that it must be seen, and wonder must be expressed at it. As for the one who distinguished between "ألم تر" (alam tara, "have you not seen") and "أرأيت" (ara'ayta, "have you seen"), after clarifying that both are shared in usage for the purpose of expressing wonder, saying that the first is linked to the very person being wondered at, so it is said: "ألم تر إلى الذي صنع كذا" (alam tara ila alladhi sana'a kadha), meaning: look at him and wonder at his condition; and the second is linked to something like the one being wondered at, so it is said: "أرأيت مثل الذي صنع كذا" (ara'ayta mithla alladhi sana'a kadha), meaning that it is of such strangeness that no like of it is seen. He has indeed preserved something, but other things escaped him, and it seems he overlooked the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Have you seen the one who denies the Recompense?﴾ (107:1). The "fa" (فاء) is for coordination with an implied antecedent required by the context, that is: "Have you considered and seen the one who disbelieved in Our manifest signs, which every one who witnesses them ought to believe in."

﴿And he said﴾, mocking them, prefacing his speech with a wicked oath, "By God, I will certainly be given﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿wealth and children﴾. That is: look at him and wonder at his unusual condition and his monstrous audacity. This is what the eloquence of the noble arrangement requires. It has been said that "أرأيت" (ara'ayta) means "inform me" (akhbir), and the "fa" is in its original sense, and the meaning is: inform (about) the account of this disbeliever following the speech of those who said, which of "the two groups is better in station" (19:73)... and so on to the end of the verse. You know that the well-known usage of "أرأيت" is in the sense of "tell me" by way of interrogation, remaining on its original sense, or being turned to what suits it of meanings, not by way of the imperative directing another to inform. It is read: (وُلْدًا) (wuldan), either as a plural of walad, like usd as the plural of asad, or as a dialectal variant of it, like al-'urb and al-'arab. And the Most High's saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 78:

﴿Has he attained knowledge of the unseen, or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?﴾ This is a rejection of his shameful statement and a demonstration of its falsehood, following the expression of astonishment at it. That is to say: has he reached such a height of greatness that he has ascended to knowledge of the unseen, which the All-Knowing, the All-Aware has reserved for Himself, so that he claims he will be given wealth and children in the Hereafter, and swears to it?

﴿Or has he taken a covenant with the Most Merciful?﴾ concerning that, for knowledge of it can only be reached by one of these two ways. The mention of the title "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahmaniyyah) serves to indicate that mercy is the cause for granting what he claims. It has been said: "the covenant" is the word of testimony (kalimat al-shahadah). It has also been said: it is righteous deeds, for God's promise of reward for them is like a covenant. This is an accommodation with the accursed one according to the literal sense of his speech, just as his speech with Khabbab was of this kind. And the words of God Most High:

﴿Nay﴾: a rebuke to him for uttering that monstrous claim, and a warning that he is in error.

﴿We shall record what he says﴾: that is, We shall make it manifest that We have recorded his statement, as in the line of verse:

*"When we trace our lineage, no base woman has borne me."*

That is, it becomes clear that I was not born of a base woman. Or the meaning is: We shall take vengeance on him as one who records a criminal's crime and keeps it against him, for the recording tablet itself scarcely delays in recording a word, as He, Mighty and Exalted, says: ﴿He does not utter a word but that with him is a watcher ready [to record it]﴾. The basis of the first meaning is treating the manifesting of a hidden thing as the bringing into being of a non-existent thing, through the common element that each is a bringing out from concealment into visibility. This makes it a sequential metaphor (*istiʿara tabʿiyya*), founded on likening the manifestation of the writing before the witnesses to its creation. The basis of the second meaning is naming a thing by its cause (*tasmiyat al-shayʾ bi-ism sababihi*), since the recording of the criminal's crime is certainly a cause of his punishment. (p-280)

﴿And We shall extend for him of the punishment an extension﴾: in place of what he claims for himself of being provided with wealth and children. That is, We shall lengthen for him the punishment that he deserves, or We shall increase his punishment and multiply it for him, because of his disbelief, his fabricating against God, Glorified is He, and his mocking of His grand signs. For this reason it is emphasized with the verbal noun, to indicate the intensity of anger.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 80:

﴿And We shall inherit﴾ by his death ﴿what he says﴾. That is: the referent (musamma) of what he says and its fulfilment (misdaq), namely the wealth and children he was given in this world. It indicates that what he says has no existing fulfilment other than what has been mentioned; that is, We shall strip from him what We gave him.

﴿And he will come to Us﴾ on the Day of Resurrection ﴿alone﴾, unaccompanied by wealth or by the children he had in the world, let alone being given more than that there. It has also been said: We shall withhold from him what he claimed he would attain in the Hereafter, and We shall give him what he deserves; but the meaning of inheritance (irth) rules this out. It has also been said: what he says refers to the statement itself, not its referent, and the meaning is that he says this statement only for as long as he is alive; when We take him, We will prevent him from saying it, and he will come to Us rejecting it, separated from it. You know well that this is based on the view that the aforementioned statement issues from him as an expression of belief, and that he persists in uttering it while hoping for its content to occur; and there is no doubt that this is impossible for one who disbelieved in the Resurrection. Rather, he said what he said as mockery, and as making the discharge of his debt conditional upon the impossible.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 81:

﴿And they have taken gods besides Allah﴾ is a report of a general offence, common to all, which follows (mustatba'a) upon the opposite of what the one they are mentioning (yarji'una) arranges for them, and its consequence is the opposite of its content. That is, they took the idols as gods, transgressing beyond Allah, exalted is He.

﴿That they might be for them a source of might﴾ means: that they might strengthen themselves through them, by being for them a means of access to Him, mighty and majestic, and intercessors with Him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 82:

﴿Nay!﴾ It is a rebuke to them for that false belief, and a denial that what they had attached their empty hopes to will come to pass.

﴿They will disavow their worship﴾, that is: the gods will deny their worship of them, by God Most High making them speak and say, "You did not worship us." Or, the disbelievers, when they witness the evil outcome of their disbelief, will deny their worship of them, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾. The meaning of God Most High's words ﴿and they will be opposed to them﴾ according to the first view: the gods in whom they hoped to find might for them will become the opposite of might, that is, humiliation and disgrace, or they will become a means of aid against them and an instrument of their punishment, as they will be made fuel for the Fire and the firewood of Hell. Or, their worship of them was a cause of their punishment. The use of ḍidd (opposite) for ʿawn (aid) is because a man's helper is opposed to his enemy and contradicts him by helping him against him. According to the second view: the disbelievers will be opposed to and enemies of the gods, disbelieving in them after they had loved them as they love God and worshipped them. The singular ḍidd is used because of the unity of the meaning on which their opposition revolves, for they are thereby like one thing, as in the words of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "They are a single hand against whoever is other than them."

It is also read as (كَلًّا) with a fatḥa on the kāf and tanwīn, by converting the alif into a nūn in pausal form (waqf), like the conversion of the alif of extension (alif al-iṭlāq) in the words of the poet:

"Lessen your blame, O reproacher, and your rebuke,
and say, if I was right, then indeed I was right."

Or the meaning is: this opinion is entirely (kullan) an opinion. It is also read as (كَلّا) with an implied verb that is explained by what follows it, that is: they will deny, nay, they will disbelieve... and so on.

(p-281) ﴿Have you not seen that We have sent the devils upon the disbelievers?﴾ This is a wonderment directed at the Messenger of God (ﷺ) at what the preceding noble verses have stated and related about these disbelievers, rebels and haughty tyrants, of the various kinds of ugly sayings and deeds, persistence in error, immersion in misguidance, excess in obstinacy, and determination in disbelief without any restraint turning them back or any inclination bending them away; and [it relates to] their unanimous rejection of the truth after its clarity and the complete absence of doubt about it. It is also an indication that all of that proceeds from them through the misguidance and seduction of the devils, not because there is any justification for it at all. The meaning of "sending the devils upon them" is either empowering them over the disbelievers and enabling them to mislead them, or assigning them as companions to them. The intent is not to express wonderment (upon him, peace) at their being sent upon them, as the linking of the sight to it might suggest; rather, the wonderment is at the states of the disbelievers insofar as these are effects of the seduction of the devils, as indicated by the words of the Exalted: ﴿They incite them with a fierce inciting﴾. For this is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl muqaddara) referring to the devils, or a resumptive statement (istiʾnāf) that comes as an answer to what arises from the beginning of the discourse, as if it were said: "What do the devils do to them then?" So it is said: "They incite them," that is: they stir them up and agitate them toward sins with intense agitation, through various kinds of whisperings and enticements. For al-azz (incitement), al-hazz (prodding) and al-istifzaz (provocation) are siblings in meaning: intense agitation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 84:

﴿So do not hasten against them﴾, i.e., that they be destroyed in accordance with what their crimes require, and that they be wiped out to the last of them, and the earth be purified of their corruptions. The "fa'" (fa, the particle of consequence) here serves to indicate that what precedes it is a prelude (mizallah) to the occurrence of what is forbidden, one that necessitates the prohibition, as in His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Indeed, this is an enemy to you and to your wife, so let him not expel you both from the Garden﴾; and His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Indeed, We are counting for them a counting﴾ is a justification for the requirement of the prohibition, by clarifying how near their destruction is. That is: do not seek to hasten their destruction, for there remain for them only days, and breaths which We are counting, counting.

On the Day We gather the God-fearing (al-muttaqin) to the Most Merciful, as a delegation (wafdan).

On the Day We gather the God-fearing: "Yawm" is in the accusative case as an adverb of time (zarfiyya), governed by a verb that comes later in the sentence and has been omitted. The verb is omitted to convey that the expression is too constrained to contain its full scope and explanation, given the utter horror of what takes place on that Day: the all-encompassing calamity and the general catastrophes. It is as if it were said: "On the Day We gather the God-fearing," meaning: We will assemble them.

To the Most Merciful: to their Lord, who overwhelms them with His vast mercy.

As a delegation (wafdan): coming to Him as delegations come to kings, awaiting their honour and bounty.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 86:

﴿And We shall drive the criminals﴾ as cattle are driven.

﴿To Hell, thirsting﴾ (wirdan), i.e., parched with thirst. For one who comes to water (warada al-ma') comes to it only out of thirst, or like the beasts that come to water. We do with both groups of actions that which the range of speech cannot fully express. It has also been said: it is in the accusative as an object of an implied verb placed in front, addressed to the Prophet of God (ﷺ), i.e., "Mention to them, by way of encouragement and warning, the day when We shall gather ..." etc. It has also been said: it is in the accusative of time (zarfiyyah), due to His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 87:

﴿They shall not possess intercession﴾. What the grandeur of the context requires, and what the eloquence of the revelation calls for, is that it be in the accusative by one of the first two readings (i'rab, grammatical case-analysis). This is a clarifying resumption (istina'f) explaining some of the matters within it that indicate its terror, and its pronoun refers back to "the servants" (al-'ibad), which is implied by the mention of the two groups, since they are confined to them. It was said: it refers to the God-fearing (al-muttaqun) specifically, and it was said: it refers to the criminals (al-mujrimun) among the unbelievers and the people of Islam. The "intercession" (al-shafa'ah) is, according to the first two, a verbal noun (masdar) from the active form, and according to the third, it should be a verbal noun from the passive form. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except one who has taken a covenant with the Most Merciful﴾, according to the first, is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil) from "they shall not possess." The position of the excepted element is either nominative as a substitute (badal), or accusative on the basic principle of exception (asl al-istithna'). The meaning: the servants do not possess the ability to intercede for others except for one who has prepared himself for it by adorning himself with faith and piety, or one who has been commanded to do so, from their saying: "The commander charged ('ahida) so-and-so with such-and-such" when he ordered him to do it. This is an encouragement for people to acquire faith and piety, which leads to attaining this rank. According to the second: it is an exception from "intercession" by omitting the annexed noun (al-mudaf), and the excepted element is accusative as a substitute, or on the basic principle of exception, i.e.: the God-fearing do not possess intercession except the intercession of one who has taken the covenant of Islam, and this is an encouragement toward Islam. According to the third: it is also an exception from "they shall not possess," and the excepted element is nominative as a substitute, or accusative on the basic principle; the meaning: the criminals do not possess the ability to have anyone intercede for them except one of them who was a Muslim.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 88:

﴿And they say: The Most Merciful has taken to Himself a son.﴾ This is a report of the transgression of the Jews and the Christians, and of those among the Arabs who claim that the angels are the daughters of Allah, exalted is He above that with a great exaltation, following on from the report of the idol-worshippers, by way of conjoining one narrative to another. And His, exalted be He, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 89:

﴿You have certainly brought a monstrous thing﴾. This is a refutation of their false claim, and an amplification of its gravity by way of iltifat (the shift in grammatical person), which indicates complete anger and intense wrath, expressing the utmost reproach and condemnation, and a recording against them of the utmost impudence, ignorance and audacity. And "al-idd" (the monstrous thing), with kasra or fatha on the initial letter, means: the great and reprehensible thing. And "al-idda" means severity, and the lowest/most urgent part of a matter. And "adanee" means it burdened me and was grievous upon me, i.e., you have committed a reprehensible and severe matter whose magnitude cannot be measured. "Ja'a" (came) and "ata" (came) are used in the sense of a verb (fi'l), and they take its transitivity; and His, the Exalted's, saying:

﴿The heavens are about to﴾ ... to the end. This is a qualifier (ṣifah) of "iddan" (a monstrous thing), or a resumptive clause (isti'naf) that explains the great magnitude of its severity and terror. It is also read as "yakādu" with the masculine verb form.

﴿they are split apart from it﴾: they split, one crack after another, from the enormity of that matter. It is also read as "yanfaṭirna" (يَنْفَطِرْنَ). The first reading (yatafaṭṭarna, يَتَفَطَّرْنَ) is more emphatic, because tafa''ala (تَفَعَّلَ) is the reflexive (muṭāwi') of fa''ala (فَعَّلَ), whereas infa'ala (انْفَعَلَ) is the reflexive of fa'ala (فَعَلَ), and because the basic sense of tafa''ul (التَّفَعُّلِ) is effort or affectation (takalluf).

﴿and the earth is split open﴾: that is, "and the earth is almost split open."

﴿and the mountains collapse﴾: that is, they fall down and are demolished. As for His words, ﴿hadda﴾ (هَدًّا), it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) emphasizing an implied verb that is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the mountains, meaning: they are crushed with crushing. Or it is a verbal noun from the passive form, emphasizing "takhirru" (تَخِرُّ) without being of the same root as its verb, since in that case it carries the sense of demolition and collapse, as if it were said: "and the mountains collapse with a collapse." Or it is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, in the accusative as a state (ḥāl), meaning "demolished"; or it is an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu), meaning "because they are crushed." This is an explanation of its being a monstrous thing. The meaning is that the terror of that dreadful event and its enormity is such that, if it were imagined in a perceptible form, those great bodies could not bear it, and would be shattered from its severity. Or its horror lies in provoking anger and calling down wrath, to such an extent that, were it not for His forbearance (ḥilm), the world would be ruined and its foundations scattered in anger at the one who uttered it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 91:

﴿That they ascribe to the Most Merciful a son﴾ is in the accusative (manṣūb) by the elision of the preposition lām, which is connected to تَكادُ (takādu, "they nearly"), or it is in the genitive (majrūr) by the implied presence of that lām. The meaning is: "The heavens nearly split apart, and the earth splits open, and the mountains collapse, because they ascribe to Him, exalted is He, a son." It has been said that the lām is connected to هَدًّا (haddan, "collapsing"). It has also been said that the clause is a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in مِنهُ (minhu, "from it"), as in the line of poetry:

"Over his generosity, Ḥātim would have been stingy with water."

It has also been said that it is the predicate (khabar) of an elided subject, meaning: "What necessitates that is that they ascribe ... etc." It has been said that it is the subject (fā'il) of هَدًّا, meaning: "The invocation of a son has collapsed it." The first view is the most preferable.

As for دَعَوْا (da'aw, "they ascribed") from the verb da'ā in the sense of "named" (sammā), which is transitive to two objects, only the second object has been mentioned, so that it encompasses everything they ascribe to Him as a son. Alternatively, it is from da'ā in the sense of "attributed" (nasaba), whose reflexive form ibtadā (ادَّعى) means "claimed for someone," i.e., "attributed himself to him." And His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 92:

﴿And it is not befitting for the Most Merciful to take a son.﴾ This is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of "they said," or "they attributed" (da'aw) is a clause affirming the falsity of their statement and the impossibility of its content being realized. That is: they said, "The Most Merciful has taken a son," or "they attributed a son to the Most Merciful." The situation, however, is that it is not befitting for Him, exalted is He, to take a son, nor would one be sought for Him even if one were sought, because it is impossible in its very nature. The use of "al-Rahman" in place of a pronoun serves to indicate the cause of the ruling, by alerting to the fact that everything other than Him, exalted is He, is either a blessing or one upon whom a blessing has been bestowed. How, then, could it be possible that He should be of the same kind as the One who is the origin of blessings and the patron of their roots and branches, so that it could be imagined that He would take Him as a son? Indeed, a people has been addressed about Him, may He be mighty and majestic, saying:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 19, verse 93:

﴿Indeed, there is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant.﴾ That is: there is none of them, of the angels or of the two weighty creations (mankind and jinn), but that he is a slave belonging to Him, returning to Him in servitude and submission. And it has been recited (ātin al-Raḥmān) in the original form, as ( آتٍ الرَّحْمَنَ).

**Surah 19, verse 94: "He has indeed encompassed them and counted them with an exact counting."**

﴿لَقَدْ أحْصاهُمْ﴾ means: He has confined them and encompassed them, such that not one of them can escape from the grasp of His knowledge, the grip of His power, and His dominion (malakut).

﴿وَعَدَّهم عَدًّا﴾ means: He counted their persons, their breaths, their actions, and everything with Him is by measure.

And all of them will come to Him on the Day of Resurrection, individually (fardan). That is, each one of them will come to Him, exalted is He, alone, apart from followers and helpers. In the use of the active participle (ātin) there is an indication that they will certainly come in this manner, which is not conveyed by the imperfect form: had it been said "yaʾtīhi," [it would not have carried this certainty].
